title: Law for Business Leaders
question: How can a leader who is not a lawyer recognize legal issues early, read agreements as allocations of risk, and know which questions belong to counsel?

overview.text: **Educational material about general legal concepts — not legal advice. Consult a qualified attorney about any specific agreement.** This week covers U.S. law in general terms. Most of the law discussed — contracts, employment, agency and corporate law — is state law that varies from state to state, and other countries, including the civil-law systems of most of Latin America, organize these subjects differently. Nothing in this week addresses any particular person, agreement or organization, and the exercises use fictional documents.

The aim is legal literacy, not legal practice. Leaders sign, approve and negotiate documents with legal consequences long before a lawyer sees them, and they decide which questions reach counsel at all. This week builds the habits that make those moments safer: reading legal questions as predictions, recognizing when a term is a rule and when it is a standard, structuring an issue, and knowing who must prove what.

The lessons move from reasoning to documents to institutions. Contracts are treated as allocations of obligation and risk. Employment terms are examined as decisions about who may leave, where they may go and who owns ideas — including a dated account of the U.S. non-compete landscape and the fate of the FTC's 2024 rule. Fiduciary duty, agency and the institutional constraints that sit above any single contract come next, and the week ends with how to work with counsel, including the basics of privilege. The Contract Lab, the case and the memo assignment all practice the same skill: a disciplined first pass that a qualified lawyer can use.

Throughout, watch the gap between what the law permits and what is wise. A clause can be enforceable and still damage trust; a legal risk can be worth taking when the business case is strong. Those judgments remain yours. Counsel supplies the forecast.

objectives: Apply an issue–rule–application–conclusion structure, with attention to burden of proof and jurisdiction, to business fact patterns.
Analyze formation, interpretation, conditions, representations, warranties and remedies in commercial agreements.
Evaluate employment terms — at-will status, restrictive covenants, confidentiality and invention assignment — against the current U.S. legal landscape and the empirical evidence.
Explain agency, fiduciary duties and the business judgment rule, and recognize institutional constraints such as regulation, labor law and league rules.
Identify, rank and explain legal and commercial issues in a fictional agreement, and frame precise questions and plain-language redlines for qualified counsel.
Judge when and how to involve counsel, including the basics of privilege and preservation.

lessons.title: Legal Reasoning for Non-Lawyers: Prediction, Rules and Proof
lessons.summary: Legal reasoning is disciplined prediction: name the issue, find the governing rule, apply it to the facts, and estimate how a decision-maker would rule and with what confidence.
objectives: Explain the prediction view of law and use it to translate legal questions into risk estimates.
Distinguish rules from standards and evaluate the trade-offs of each in contracts and internal policies.
Apply an issue–rule–application–conclusion structure to a business fact pattern, including the burden of proof.
Identify when precedent and jurisdiction make a confident legal conclusion premature.
lessons.executive: Lawyers are paid to predict, not to pronounce. Holmes described the law as a forecast of what courts will actually do, and that view converts most legal questions into the language executives already use: probability, consequence, cost and time. Two tools make you a better consumer of legal judgment. First, notice whether a question is governed by a rule, clear in advance but sometimes unfair at the edges, or a standard, fair in principle but uncertain until someone decides. Second, structure every issue as issue, rule, application and conclusion, then ask who must prove what, and how convincingly. You will not replace counsel; you will ask sharper questions and recognize when “it depends” is the honest answer.

explore.text: **Educational material about general legal concepts — not legal advice. Consult a qualified attorney about any specific agreement.** This week is general, U.S.-centric education. Law differs across states and countries, changes over time, and turns on facts no course can see.

A product director at a mid-sized software company plans to launch a feature next month and asks the company's lawyer a simple question: “Are we allowed to do this?” The lawyer answers, “It depends.” The director hears evasion. The lawyer meant something precise. The answer depends on which facts are true, which jurisdiction's law applies, how a regulator or judge would characterize the feature, and how much risk the company is willing to carry while it finds out. (Hypothetical.)
Before reading on, list three things the lawyer's answer might depend on. Which of them could the director find out herself this week, without a lawyer?
The prophecies of what the courts will do in fact, and nothing more pretentious, are what I mean by the law.

Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. offered that definition in an 1897 address later published in the *Harvard Law Review*. He argued that, for practical purposes, the law is a forecast of how public force will be applied. He asked readers to look at law as a “bad man” would: someone indifferent to morality who cares only about material consequences. The point was not that people should behave badly. It was that the perspective separates what the law actually requires from what we wish it required, and from what we think is right.

This week treats that idea as a working tool rather than a philosophy. When you ask counsel a question, you are asking for a forecast. Good forecasts come with conditions, ranges and stated confidence. Poor ones arrive as verdicts. Your job is to supply the facts that sharpen the forecast and to combine it with the business judgment that remains yours.

understand.text: Where legal rules come from

understand.title: Prerequisite: how U.S. law is organized

blocks.text: U.S. law comes from several layered sources. Constitutions set the outer limits. Legislatures enact statutes. Agencies issue regulations under authority delegated by statutes. Courts decide disputes, interpret statutes and regulations, and, in fields such as contracts and torts, develop the *common law* through their decisions. Contracts add one more layer: private rules the parties create for themselves, enforceable to the extent public law allows.

The United States has a federal system and fifty state systems. Most contract, employment, agency and corporate law is state law, which is why the same clause can be enforceable in one state and void in another. Trial courts find facts and apply the law; appellate courts review legal questions and write the opinions that become precedent. Outside the United States the structure can differ sharply: most of Latin America and continental Europe follow civil-law traditions built around comprehensive codes rather than judge-made common law.

understand.text: Courts in common-law systems follow *precedent*, the doctrine of *stare decisis*. A court is bound by earlier decisions of higher courts in its own jurisdiction on materially similar questions and treats decisions from elsewhere as persuasive at most. Much legal argument is therefore argument by analogy. One side says the present case is like an earlier one; the other *distinguishes* it by pointing to a fact that should change the outcome. When a lawyer says “that case is distinguishable,” you are hearing a claim that a specific fact matters, and you can ask which one.
Rules and standards

Legal commands come in two broad forms. A **rule** fixes the content of the law before anyone acts: “Invoices are payable within 30 days.” A **standard** leaves the content to be determined after the fact: “Invoices are payable within a reasonable time.” Louis Kaplow's economic analysis frames the choice as a question of when the work of giving content to the law is done. Rules cost more to write well, because someone must anticipate situations in advance. Standards cost more to apply, because each party, adviser and judge must work out what “reasonable” means in each dispute.

Kaplow's analysis yields a practical heuristic. When the same kind of conduct happens often and looks similar each time, the up-front cost of a rule is spread over many cases, and rules tend to win. When situations are rare and varied, standards tend to win, because writing an accurate rule for each would cost more than it saves. He also argues that people can learn what a rule requires before they act, so behavior tracks rules more closely than standards whose content appears only later.

understand.text: Who must prove what

Every legal dispute also has a *burden of proof*: which party must persuade the decision-maker, and how convincingly. In most U.S. civil cases, including contract disputes, the party bringing the claim must prove it by a *preponderance of the evidence*, meaning more likely than not. Criminal prosecutions require proof *beyond a reasonable doubt*. Some civil matters, such as fraud claims in many jurisdictions, require *clear and convincing evidence*, a level between the two.

For an executive, the burden matters in two ways. It tells you which side loses when the evidence is evenly balanced. And it tells you which records you need now. If your organization would have to show that a contractor's work was defective, or that a personnel decision was made for legitimate reasons, the time to create that evidence is when you act, not when a dispute begins. Contemporaneous notes, emails that state reasons, and documented processes are often worth more than any argument made later.
A structure for issue spotting

Law students learn to organize analysis as **IRAC**: Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion. IRAC is a teaching and writing heuristic, not a theory of how judges decide. Its value for non-lawyers is discipline. It forces you to name the precise question, to separate the governing rule from your opinion of it, to apply the rule to the facts that matter, including the ones that cut against you, and to reach a conclusion you could defend. APERTURE adds a fifth step for executive use: the consequence, and your confidence in the conclusion.

steps.label: Issue
steps.text: State the precise legal question the facts raise.

steps.label: Rule
steps.text: Identify the governing rule or standard, its source and its jurisdiction.

steps.label: Application
steps.text: Apply the rule to the material facts, including facts that cut the other way.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.text: State the likely outcome and what would change it.

steps.label: Consequence and confidence
steps.text: Estimate the stakes and the probability; decide whether counsel is needed.

understand.title: Methodological note: why rules and standards blur

blocks.text: Kaplow separates the rule-versus-standard choice from the question of how detailed a law should be. A detailed standard that lists six factors for a court to weigh can leave the outcome just as open as a one-word standard, and a short rule can be perfectly precise. Complexity and timing are different dimensions.

In practice, rules acquire exceptions and standards acquire precedents. A “reasonable notice” standard applied in many decisions develops a working range that behaves almost like a rule, while a bright-line rule surrounded by exceptions behaves like a standard. When you read a clause, ask three questions: how much of its content will be supplied after the fact, by whom, and with what incentives. A standard interpreted by a neutral court is different from a standard interpreted “in the Company's sole discretion.”

challenge.text: The prediction view has limits. Legal philosophers have objected that it describes law from the outside, from the standpoint of someone trying to avoid sanctions, and misses why officials and citizens treat legal rules as reasons for action rather than prices. For an executive, the practical risk is different: treating every obligation as a cost to be priced can erode the trust that makes contracts and organizations work. Holmes's “bad man” is a diagnostic lens, not a model for conduct.

Issue spotting by non-lawyers carries its own risk. A little structure produces confidence faster than it produces accuracy. You can recognize that a non-compete raises an enforceability question without being able to answer it, because the answer depends on state statutes, recent decisions, the specific facts and a court's discretion to narrow or refuse a clause. The goal of this week is to recognize issues and frame questions, not to resolve them.

Legal and ethical are different tests. Holmes separated law from morals so that lawyers would not confuse what a rule says with what they believe it ought to say. Executives need the separation in the opposite direction as well: an action can be lawful and still be wrong, imprudent or corrosive to trust. Week 13 returns to that gap.

Finally, the rule-versus-standard trade-off is not only a legal matter. Internal policies face the same choice. A travel policy with fixed daily amounts is a rule; “spend responsibly” is a standard. A gift policy that names a dollar limit is a rule; “avoid conflicts of interest” is a standard. Organizations that rely only on standards create uncertainty and uneven enforcement, and people learn that outcomes depend on who decides. Organizations that rely only on rules invite gaming at the edges and frustrate people whose situations the rule did not foresee.

apply.text: Worked example: a consultant's “guarantee”

A partner at a consulting firm emails a hospital client: “We will deliver the staffing model by March 1 — guaranteed.” The signed engagement letter says the firm will use “commercially reasonable efforts” to meet “target dates,” and it contains a clause stating that the letter is the parties' entire agreement. The model arrives on March 20. The hospital's chief operating officer asks whether the firm breached. (Hypothetical.)

items: **Issue.** Did the firm promise delivery by March 1, or only reasonable efforts toward a target date?

**Rule.** Contract terms are generally read as written; an *entire agreement* (integration) clause can limit the weight of statements outside the signed document; “commercially reasonable efforts” is a standard, not a fixed deadline.

**Application.** The guarantee appeared in an email. If it was sent before the letter was signed, the integration clause probably weakens it. If it was sent afterward, the hospital could argue it modified the agreement, and the firm would answer that it was reassurance, not a new promise. On the efforts standard, the firm will argue its efforts were reasonable; the hospital, as claimant, would need evidence that they were not.
**Conclusion.** A breach claim based on the guarantee is uncertain; a claim based on the efforts standard turns on facts about what caused the delay.

**Consequence and confidence.** Twenty days of delay may matter less than the relationship. A sensible path is to document the delay's costs, ask counsel one narrow question about the email's effect, and use the uncertainty in a commercial conversation rather than a legal one.

apply.text: Notice what the structure did. It turned an emotional question (“they promised!”) into three answerable ones: what exactly was promised, in which document, and who can prove what about the delay.

apply.title: Executive twist: counsel gives you a number

blocks.text: Your general counsel says a lawsuit against a former vendor has “about a 60 percent chance” of success. Treat the number as a forecast, not a fact. Ask what it rests on: comparable cases, the particular judge, or professional intuition. Ask what range would not surprise counsel, and which new fact would move the estimate most. Then ask what winning would be worth after fees, time and management attention, and how likely settlement is before trial. A 60 percent chance of winning less than the cost of litigating is a losing proposition. You are combining a legal forecast with a business valuation, and the second part is your job, not counsel's.

check.prompt: A company’s expense policy says employees may spend “a reasonable amount” on client dinners. Reimbursement disputes are frequent and the situations are very similar. What does Kaplow’s analysis of rules and standards suggest?

options.text: Keep the standard; it adapts to each dinner and avoids unfairness at the edges.
Consider a rule, such as a per-person cap with an approval route for exceptions, because frequent and similar situations spread the cost of writing the rule across many cases.
The choice between rules and standards matters only for statutes, not internal policies.
Replace it with a longer standard that lists factors, which is equivalent to a rule.

check.explanation: Kaplow argues that rules are costlier to create but cheaper to apply, so they tend to be efficient when the regulated conduct is frequent and similar. Recurring, near-identical dinner reimbursements fit that description; a cap with an exception route keeps most of the certainty while handling unusual cases.

optionFeedback.a: Adaptability is the standard’s strength, but with frequent, similar disputes the repeated cost of deciding what “reasonable” means each time is exactly what a rule saves.
optionFeedback.c: The same trade-off applies to any system of commands, including contracts and internal policies.
optionFeedback.d: Kaplow distinguishes detail from timing: a factor list is still a standard whose content is supplied after the fact.

check.prompt: In a U.S. civil contract dispute, a court finds the evidence on whether a shipment was delivered on time to be exactly balanced. Who typically loses on that point?

options.text: The defendant, because doubts are resolved against the party accused of breach.
The party that bears the burden of proof on that point, usually the party bringing the claim.
Neither; the court must order a new trial when evidence is balanced.
The party that drafted the contract, under the rule that ambiguity is construed against the drafter.

check.explanation: Under the preponderance standard, the party with the burden must show its version is more likely than not. Evidence in perfect balance does not meet that standard, so the party carrying the burden — usually the claimant — loses on that point. That is why contemporaneous records matter.

optionFeedback.a: In civil cases there is no general presumption against the defendant; the claimant usually carries the burden.
optionFeedback.c: Balanced evidence is resolved by the burden of proof, not by ordering a new trial.
optionFeedback.d: Construing ambiguity against the drafter concerns the meaning of words, not disputed facts such as delivery dates.

lessons.title: Contracts: Formation, Meaning, Risk and Remedies
lessons.summary: A contract is a set of enforceable promises whose value lies less in the threat of a lawsuit than in how clearly it allocates obligations, conditions and risks before anything goes wrong.
objectives: Identify the elements of contract formation and explain the role of consideration and its substitutes.
Distinguish promises, conditions, representations and warranties, and explain why the difference matters when something goes wrong.
Apply basic interpretation principles to an ambiguous clause.
Explain expectation damages, foreseeability and mitigation, and use them to estimate exposure.
lessons.executive: Most commercial relationships never see a courtroom, and many run on handshakes layered over documents nobody rereads. Contracts still matter because they decide, in advance, who must do what, under which conditions, who carries which risks, and what happens when performance fails. The legal core is compact: an offer, an acceptance and a bargained-for exchange; terms read in context, with genuine ambiguity often resolved against the drafter; and remedies that aim to give the injured party the benefit of the bargain, limited by foreseeability and the duty to mitigate. Executives add the most value by insisting on clarity in scope, conditions and risk allocation, where good relationships most often break.

explore.text: **Educational material about general legal concepts — not legal advice. Consult a qualified attorney about any specific agreement.** Contract law in the United States is mainly state law; this lesson describes general principles, and the contract's own terms and the governing jurisdiction can change any of them.

In the early 1960s the law professor Stewart Macaulay, publishing in a leading sociology journal, reported what businesspeople told him about how they managed their deals. His finding unsettled contract scholars. Businesspeople often did not plan their exchanges completely, and they seldom used legal sanctions to adjust relationships or settle disputes. They relied instead on reputation, repeat dealing and a shared sense of what fair practice required.
If businesspeople rarely sue, why do organizations spend so much on drafting contracts? Write down two purposes a contract serves that have nothing to do with litigation.

One answer is that a contract matters most when the relationship fails: when key people leave, a company is acquired, budgets are cut or a product causes harm. Another is that drafting forces the parties to discover disagreements while they are still cheap to resolve. A third is that contracts coordinate people who were not in the room — the finance team that pays invoices, the engineers who deliver, the successor executive who inherits the deal. This lesson teaches the legal core so you can read any contract as a map of what each side expects when things go wrong.

understand.title: Prerequisite: the anatomy of a commercial contract

blocks.text: Most commercial contracts share a shape. A preamble names the parties. Recitals (“Whereas…”) describe the background and usually create no obligations by themselves. Definitions give capitalized terms fixed meanings that apply throughout. Operative clauses state what each side must do. Risk clauses — warranties, indemnities, limitations of liability, insurance — allocate losses. Term and termination clauses govern duration and exit. The “boilerplate” at the end — governing law, notices, assignment, entire agreement — looks routine and often decides disputes. Schedules or statements of work hold the commercial detail, and conflicts between them and the main body should be resolved by an order-of-precedence clause.

understand.text: Formation: offer, acceptance, consideration

Under the U.S. common law of contracts, synthesized in the American Law Institute's *Restatement (Second) of Contracts*, a contract is formed when one party makes an **offer** — a manifestation of willingness to enter a bargain that invites acceptance — and the other **accepts** it, and the exchange is supported by **consideration**: each side's promise or performance is bargained for in exchange for the other's. A promise to make a gift lacks consideration and is generally not enforceable as a contract. Courts look at objective manifestations — what the parties said and did — rather than private intentions.

Where consideration is missing, courts sometimes enforce a promise anyway under **promissory estoppel**: the promisor should reasonably have expected the promise to induce action, the promisee did rely on it, and injustice can be avoided only by enforcing it. The doctrine matters in employment and business settings when someone relocates, resigns or turns down other work in reliance on a promise that never became a formal contract. Courts apply it cautiously, and recovery is sometimes limited to the losses caused by the reliance.

Other formation requirements include capacity and a lawful purpose, and certain categories of agreement must be evidenced by a signed writing under statutes of frauds. Sales of goods are governed in most states by Article 2 of the Uniform Commercial Code, which relaxes some common-law formation rules; services agreements, including consulting and employment contracts, are generally governed by the common law.
Meaning: interpretation and ambiguity

Interpretation begins with the words, read in the context of the whole agreement and its commercial purpose. Courts generally prefer readings that give effect to every term, treat specific terms as weightier than general ones, and give weight to the parties' prior course of dealing and to trade usage. When a term remains genuinely ambiguous, many courts construe it against the party that drafted it, the principle known as *contra proferentem*, usually as a tie-breaker of last resort rather than a first move. Contracts also carry an implied duty of good faith and fair dealing in their performance and enforcement, which limits how a party may use discretion the contract gives it.

Ambiguity has two common sources. *Lexical* ambiguity arises when a word has more than one meaning: does “net revenue” mean before or after refunds? *Structural* ambiguity arises from syntax: does “within 30 days of delivery and acceptance” run from delivery, from acceptance, or from whichever is later? Each can be fixed by a definition or a worked example in the document, which costs a sentence now and can save a dispute later.
Promises, conditions, representations and warranties

understand.text: The categories matter because the consequences differ. If a duty depends on a condition that never occurs, the party is excused, not in breach. If a representation was false when made, the other party may have a misrepresentation claim that, in some circumstances, lets it rescind the deal. A warranty turns a statement into a promise with a remedy, so the injured party need not prove the speaker was careless. Sophisticated parties negotiate hard over *knowledge qualifiers* (“to Seller's knowledge”), *materiality qualifiers* and survival periods, because each shifts who bears the cost of facts nobody knew.
Remedies: what a court can give

The usual remedy for breach is money damages measured by the **expectation interest**: the amount that puts the injured party in the position it would have occupied had the contract been performed. Courts can instead protect the **reliance interest** (costs incurred in reliance on the contract) or the **restitution interest** (benefits conferred on the other side). Damages are limited by foreseeability — losses that were not a probable result of breach when the contract was made are generally not recoverable — by the requirement of reasonable certainty, and by the injured party's duty to take reasonable steps to mitigate. Orders to perform, called *specific performance*, are exceptional and are rarely available for personal services.

understand.title: Methodological note: what the Restatement is, and is not

blocks.text: The *Restatement (Second) of Contracts*, published by the American Law Institute in 1981 after work led by the reporters Robert Braucher and then E. Allan Farnsworth, states the common law of contracts as black-letter rules with comments and illustrations. It is a secondary authority. Courts frequently cite and adopt its sections, but a section binds no court until that jurisdiction adopts it, and states differ on important points. When a lawyer says “the Restatement position is…”, the next question is whether your jurisdiction follows it.

Treat the Restatement as a well-organized summary of the mainstream, not as a statute. For goods, start with the Uniform Commercial Code as enacted in the relevant state; for anything outside the United States, start fresh with local counsel.

challenge.text: How much does formal contract law matter? Macaulay's interviews suggest that in ongoing commercial relationships, legal sanctions are rarely used and planning is often incomplete; reputation and relationships do much of the work. The doctrinal tradition summarized in the Restatement assumes that enforceable promises and court remedies anchor commercial expectations. Later commentators have argued that Macaulay's headline finding needs specification: formal contracts may matter little during a healthy relationship and a great deal at its end, in one-off transactions, or when the parties' interests diverge. His evidence came from interviews rather than measured outcomes, in a particular period and industry mix. Both views can be true at different points in the same relationship.

A second limit concerns remedies. Expectation damages sound complete, but litigation is slow and expensive, U.S. courts generally do not award attorneys' fees to the winner unless a contract or statute provides for them, and losses that are hard to prove may not be recovered at all. In practice, the contract's own mechanisms — payment milestones, service credits, termination rights, escrows and liability caps — often determine what a party actually receives. Read those mechanisms as the real remedy.

A third limit is the cost of completeness. A contract that anticipates every contingency is expensive to negotiate and can signal distrust. Economists describe contracts that leave contingencies unaddressed as *incomplete*, and the right degree of completeness depends on the stakes, the predictability of the future, and how far both sides can rely on relationship and reputation. This is Lesson 1's rules-versus-standards trade-off in another form.

apply.text: Worked examples: three clauses, three industries

**Technology.** A cloud-software agreement says the provider “will use commercially reasonable efforts to maintain 99.9 percent monthly availability” and that service credits are the customer's “sole and exclusive remedy” for downtime. The number looks like a rule, but the efforts language makes it a standard, and the exclusive-remedy clause means a long outage may yield only a modest credit. The questions to raise: does the remedy match the business harm, and is there a right to terminate after repeated failures? (Hypothetical.)

**Healthcare.** A hospital signs with a staffing agency whose contract makes payment due “within 30 days of invoice, subject to the hospital's verification of hours.” Verification is a condition with no deadline or procedure, so the hospital can delay payment almost indefinitely and the agency's remedy is uncertain. One sentence — “hours are deemed verified unless disputed in writing within ten business days” — turns an open condition into a rule. (Hypothetical.)

**Finance.** In an acquisition, the seller represents that “there is no pending or threatened litigation.” After closing, the buyer learns that a former employee had sent a demand letter. Whether this breaches the representation depends on whether a demand letter counts as threatened litigation and on any knowledge qualifier. What the buyer actually recovers depends on the indemnity clause: its cap, its survival period, and its basket, a threshold of loss below which no claim can be made. (Hypothetical.)
Worked exposure estimate

items: A consultant has a 12-month engagement at $15,000 per month with no right for the client to terminate for convenience. The client ends it without justification after month 4 and stops paying. (Synthetic numbers.)
Unpaid fees for the remaining eight months: 8 × $15,000 = $120,000.
She finds comparable replacement work starting in month 7 at $10,000 per month: 6 × $10,000 = $60,000 earned in months 7–12.
A simplified expectation measure, ignoring costs saved, interest and legal fees: $120,000 − $60,000 = $60,000.

Now change one clause. If the contract allowed either party to terminate for convenience on 30 days' notice, expected damages would be roughly one month's fee. The termination clause, not the damages doctrine, sets most of the exposure.

The questions are the same as in any industry. Is the scope a rule or a standard? Which duties are conditional, and who controls the condition? What did the vendor represent about accuracy, data security or certifications, and is that statement a representation, a warranty or merely marketing material? If the vendor fails, what does the contract actually give the organization, net of caps and exclusive-remedy language?

apply.title: Executive twist: the “non-binding” letter of intent

blocks.text: Before many deals, the parties sign a letter of intent or term sheet that says it is non-binding. Read it anyway. Such letters commonly make certain sections binding — confidentiality, exclusivity periods during which you may not negotiate with anyone else, expense allocation, and sometimes governing law. An exclusivity clause can cost you your best alternative for sixty days. Ask which sections bind, for how long, and whether the non-binding sections could still be cited later as evidence of what the parties agreed. The executive judgment is whether the leverage you give up is worth the momentum you gain.

retain.text: A contract forms through offer, acceptance and bargained-for consideration, with promissory estoppel as a narrow substitute. Its words are read in context, and genuine ambiguity may be resolved against the drafter. Promises, conditions, representations and warranties fail in different ways. Remedies aim at the benefit of the bargain but are limited by foreseeability, certainty and mitigation — and, in practice, by the contract's own caps, exclusive remedies and termination rights.

Why might a warranty be more valuable to a buyer than a representation covering the same fact?
In the exposure example, which single clause changed the consultant's expected damages most, and why?

takeaways: Formation requires offer, acceptance and bargained-for consideration; promissory estoppel can enforce some promises without consideration.
Interpretation starts with the words in context; genuine ambiguity is often resolved against the drafter, as a last resort.

Expectation damages aim at the benefit of the bargain, limited by foreseeability, certainty and mitigation — and by the contract’s own caps, exclusive remedies and termination rights.

check.prompt: A licensing agreement says: “Licensee’s obligation to pay the milestone fee arises only if the product receives regulatory approval by June 30.” Approval arrives in August, and the licensee declines to pay. Which statement best reflects general contract principles?

options.text: The licensee breached by refusing to pay a fee it promised.
Approval by June 30 was a condition; because it did not occur, the duty to pay the milestone fee did not arise, unless the condition was waived or other terms provide otherwise.
The condition is void because it produces a harsh result for the licensor.
The licensee owes reliance damages because the licensor relied on the fee.

check.explanation: The clause makes payment depend on an event (approval by a date). When a condition does not occur, the dependent duty never becomes due, so non-payment is not a breach. Waiver, other clauses or doctrines that excuse conditions can matter, but the starting analysis is the condition.

optionFeedback.a: This treats the fee as an unconditional promise; the words “arises only if” create a condition.
optionFeedback.c: Courts sometimes relieve parties of conditions to avoid forfeiture, but conditions are not void merely because they are harsh.
optionFeedback.d: Reliance damages are a remedy for breach or for promissory estoppel; neither is established when a condition simply failed.

check.prompt: A nonprofit’s program director tells an independent trainer: “Keep June free and we’ll hire you to run the summer program.” The trainer declines two other engagements. options.text: Contra proferentem, because the nonprofit chose the words.
Promissory estoppel, because the trainer reasonably relied on the promise to her detriment.
The business judgment rule, because hiring decisions are business judgments.
Expectation damages under a written contract, because the parties agreed on a program.

check.explanation: The facts suggest a promise, foreseeable reliance (declining other work) and detriment, without a formal bargained-for contract. Promissory estoppel is the doctrine designed for that pattern; whether it succeeds depends on how definite the promise was and on the jurisdiction.

optionFeedback.a: Contra proferentem resolves ambiguity in contract language; the problem here is whether an enforceable promise exists at all.
optionFeedback.c: The business judgment rule concerns judicial review of directors’ decisions, not a third party’s claim on a promise.
optionFeedback.d: There is no written contract, and whether a contract was formed is exactly what is in doubt.

lessons.title: Employment Agreements, Restrictive Covenants and Who Owns the Work
lessons.summary: Employment terms that look like boilerplate — at-will status, confidentiality, invention assignment and restrictive covenants — decide who may leave, where they may go and who owns what they create.
objectives: Explain at-will employment and its main exceptions in general terms.
Distinguish non-compete, non-solicitation, confidentiality and invention-assignment clauses and the interests each protects.
Describe the U.S. non-compete landscape as of late 2026, including the fate of the FTC’s 2024 rule, and state the limits of any such summary.
Evaluate the evidence on non-competes’ effects and identify narrower alternatives.
lessons.executive: An employment agreement allocates three scarce things: the freedom to leave, the freedom to compete and the ownership of ideas. In most of the United States employment is at will, so the clauses that operate after departure carry much of the weight. Non-competes are governed mainly by state law, which ranges from near-total refusal to enforce them to statutes that widened enforceability in 2025. The FTC’s 2024 nationwide ban was set aside by a federal court in August 2024 and abandoned by the agency in 2025. The best evidence suggests non-competes reduce mobility, especially for specialists, and are rarely negotiated. Narrower tools — confidentiality, client non-solicitation, garden leave and precise invention assignment — often protect the same interests at lower cost.

explore.text: **Educational material about general legal concepts — not legal advice. Consult a qualified attorney about any specific agreement.** Employment law varies by state, by country and by occupation, and the law on non-competes in particular has changed repeatedly in recent years. Dates below are given so you can tell how current each statement is.
Before reading on, estimate two numbers: the share of U.S. workers currently bound by a non-compete, and the share of those workers who say they negotiated over it.

A nationally representative survey of 11,505 U.S. labor force participants, published by Evan Starr, J. J. Prescott and Norman Bishara in 2021, estimated that about 18 percent were bound by a non-compete and 38 percent had agreed to at least one at some point. Non-competes appeared in high-paying jobs but also in low-wage jobs, and even in states whose courts will not enforce them. Only about 10 percent of respondents said they had negotiated over the clause, and roughly one-third were first presented with it after they had already accepted the job offer.

Those numbers describe a term that is common, rarely negotiated and sometimes unenforceable where it is used. That combination is a signal: such a clause may work less through courts than through the behavior of people who believe it binds them, and of employers who would rather not hire someone with a possible dispute attached.

understand.text: The default: employment at will

In most U.S. jurisdictions, employment without a fixed term is presumed to be **at will**: either party may end it at any time, for any lawful reason or none, without liability. The presumption has important limits. Employers may not terminate for reasons that statutes forbid, such as discrimination on protected characteristics or retaliation for protected activity; many states recognize exceptions for terminations that violate public policy; and an individual contract can promise more, such as a fixed term or termination only for defined cause.

Two further qualifications matter. Where employees are represented by a union, the collective bargaining agreement usually replaces at-will status with “just cause” protection and a grievance procedure. And outside the United States, at-will employment is unusual: many countries, including most of Latin America, require notice, severance or both. Because the relationship can end quickly, the clauses that operate *after* it ends — severance, release, restrictive covenants, confidentiality and ownership of work — often carry more economic weight than the clauses that describe the job.

understand.title: Prerequisite: the four main types of intellectual property

blocks.text: **Copyright** protects original works of authorship — including software code, reports and presentations — once they are fixed in a tangible form. **Patents** protect new, useful and non-obvious inventions for a limited term after examination by the patent office. **Trademarks** protect names and symbols that identify the source of goods or services. **Trade secrets** protect valuable information kept secret through reasonable efforts — models, methods, customer lists, formulas — for as long as secrecy lasts. Most of what knowledge workers create at work falls under copyright or trade-secret law rather than patents.

understand.text: The clauses that follow you out the door

understand.caption: Common post-employment and ownership clauses
rows: Working for, or starting, a competing business for a period and area
Trade secrets, client relationships, training investment
Duration, geography, definition of “competitor,” enforceability under state law
Soliciting the employer's clients or customers
Who counts as a client; whether accepting unsolicited business is covered
Breadth; scrutiny of no-poach arrangements between firms
Duration; whether public information and general skill are excluded
Who owns work product and inventions
Ownership of what the employer pays for
Work outside the job, on personal time, or created before employment
Working elsewhere during a paid notice period
understand.note: Original teaching synthesis. Names, combinations and enforceability vary by state and country.

understand.text: Where non-competes are enforceable, courts typically ask whether the restraint protects a legitimate business interest — trade secrets or customer goodwill, rather than simply avoiding competition — and whether its duration, geographic reach and scope of activity are reasonable. States differ on what to do with an overbroad clause: some courts narrow it to a reasonable scope, some strike only the offending words, and some refuse to enforce it at all. That variation is one reason employers draft broadly and one reason workers cannot easily tell what binds them.
The landscape as of November 2026

Non-compete law in the United States is predominantly state law, and it is moving. Practitioner summaries commonly list California, Minnesota, North Dakota and Oklahoma among the states that refuse to enforce most employee non-competes, each with exceptions such as the sale of a business. Many other states enforce reasonable non-competes but restrict them by income thresholds, advance-notice requirements or occupation. In 2025 the trend split. Wyoming enacted a statute, effective July 1, 2025, voiding most non-competes with exceptions that include the sale of a business and executive roles. Florida's CHOICE Act, effective in July 2025, moved the other way, widening the enforceability of certain non-compete and garden-leave agreements for covered workers above a wage threshold. Any list like this dates quickly; treat it as orientation, never as a statement of current law in a particular state.

steps.label: January 2023
steps.text: The FTC proposes a rule treating most worker non-competes as an unfair method of competition.

steps.label: May 7, 2024
steps.text: Final rule published in the Federal Register, scheduled to take effect September 4, 2024.

steps.label: August 20, 2024
steps.text: A federal district court in Texas (Ryan LLC v. FTC) sets the rule aside: the FTC lacked statutory authority and the rule was arbitrary and capricious.

steps.label: September 5, 2025
steps.text: The Commission votes 3–1 to dismiss its appeals and accede to vacatur.

steps.label: February 2026
steps.text: The vacated rule is removed from the Code of Federal Regulations; the FTC says it will pursue individual cases under Section 5.

understand.text: Two points about this history are easy to miss. First, the court's decision turned on the agency's authority and its rulemaking, not on a finding that non-competes are good for workers or the economy. Second, the end of the rule did not end federal attention: the FTC has said it will bring individual enforcement actions against non-competes it views as unfair methods of competition, and state law continues to govern enforceability. Anyone who says non-competes are “dead” or “fully back” is oversimplifying.
Who owns the work

Under U.S. copyright law, works created by employees within the scope of their employment are generally *works made for hire*, owned by the employer. Work by independent contractors is different: the contractor generally owns the copyright unless a signed writing assigns it or the work falls within limited statutory categories and the parties agree in writing that it is a work made for hire. That is why consulting agreements contain assignment clauses, and why the wording of those clauses matters.

Employment agreements commonly add an invention-assignment clause covering patentable inventions and other work product, and a confidentiality clause covering information. Some states limit how far an invention-assignment clause can reach into inventions developed entirely on the employee's own time, without the employer's resources, and unrelated to its business; counsel can say whether such a statute applies. The practical safeguard on both sides is a schedule of prior and excluded projects, attached at signing, and a clear definition of the employer's line of business.

understand.title: Methodological note: reading the non-compete evidence

blocks.text: Survey evidence such as Starr, Prescott and Bishara's describes prevalence, timing and negotiation well. But the associations it reports between enforceability and wages are observational: states that enforce non-competes differ from those that do not in industry mix, labor markets and many other ways.

Matt Marx, Deborah Strumsky and Lee Fleming used a natural experiment. Michigan reversed its policy of not enforcing non-competes in 1985. Comparing inventors in Michigan with inventors in states that continued not to enforce, a difference-in-differences design, they estimated that mobility fell about 8 percent after the reversal, with larger declines — around 15 to 16 percent at one standard deviation above the mean — for inventors with firm-specific skills and for specialists in narrow technical fields.

The design is stronger for causal inference than a cross-sectional comparison, but its scope is narrow: one state, one period, one occupation, and an outcome — moving between employers — that is not the same as wages, innovation or welfare. Week 4's questions apply directly: what is the counterfactual, what was measured, and how far does the result travel?

challenge.text: Do non-competes help or harm? The case for them is that they protect investments that would otherwise be underprovided: an employer may hesitate to train people or share sensitive information if a competitor can hire them the next day. The case against is that they suppress mobility, wages and the spread of knowledge. The evidence leans toward harm to mobility but is not one-sided. Michigan's reversal reduced inventor mobility, especially for specialists. Starr and colleagues found relatively lower wages where enforcement is easier, yet also found that workers told about a non-compete before accepting an offer fared better than those told afterward — a pattern consistent with some genuine bargaining when the term is disclosed early. The FTC's rulemaking argued for broad harm; the court that set the rule aside did not decide that question.

There is also a gap between enforceability and effect. A clause a court would refuse to enforce can still deter a person from taking a job, deter a new employer from hiring, or prompt a costly letter from the former employer's lawyer. When you assess a restrictive covenant — on either side of the table — its practical reach matters as much as its legal validity.

Invention-assignment clauses face a fairness tension of their own. Employers want to own what they pay for and to avoid disputes about when an idea was conceived. Employees, especially those who build tools, write or teach outside work, want room for independent work. Broad “everything you conceive during employment” language solves the employer's problem by creating the employee's. A narrower definition tied to the employer's business, plus an excluded-projects schedule, often serves both — and reduces the chance that a court narrows the clause in a way neither side planned.

apply.text: Worked example: an offer with strings

A senior data engineer receives an offer from a payments company. The base salary is above market. The agreement includes a 24-month non-compete covering “any business in the financial technology sector, worldwide”; a 12-month non-solicitation of clients and employees; confidentiality “in perpetuity” with no exclusions; and an invention-assignment clause covering “all inventions conceived during employment, whether or not on Company time.” The engineer maintains an open-source library unrelated to payments. (Hypothetical.)

items: **Non-compete breadth.** “Financial technology” and “worldwide” are broad. Enforceability depends on the governing law and on where the engineer lives and works; even an unenforceable clause may deter future employers.
**Non-solicitation.** Twelve months limited to clients the engineer actually served is a common, narrower protection; “any client of the Company” reaches much further.

**Confidentiality.** Perpetual protection is defensible for trade secrets but overbroad for ordinary business information, and standard exclusions — public information, prior knowledge, independent development, legally required disclosure — are missing.
**Invention assignment.** The open-source library should be listed as an excluded prior project; otherwise its ownership becomes contestable the moment the engineer improves it during employment.

apply.text: A reasonable agenda, from the engineer's side, starts by asking which interests the non-compete is meant to protect, then proposes narrower tools that protect them: a client non-solicit limited to accounts the engineer served, a confidentiality clause with standard exclusions, and a prior-inventions schedule. Whether to push, and how hard, is a judgment about leverage and priorities (Week 7) and about questions only a lawyer licensed in the relevant state can answer.

Professional sports organizations face a distinctive version of these questions. Coaches, analysts and medical staff move between organizations often, carry knowledge of methods and data, and sometimes build their own tools. The same distinctions apply: which information is genuinely confidential and protected by reasonable secrecy measures; who owns models, code and reports produced on the job; and whether a restriction on future work protects a legitimate interest or simply raises the cost of leaving. A department leader can prevent many disputes by setting clear expectations at hiring — what belongs to the organization, what belongs to the individual, and what happens to each at departure — rather than discovering the answers during an exit interview.

apply.title: Executive twist: the request for blanket non-competes

blocks.text: Leadership asks you to require non-competes for every new hire in your department. Before agreeing, ask which roles hold information or relationships that would cause real harm if they moved to a competitor, and how often that has happened. For other roles, a non-compete may add legal risk, slow hiring and deter strong candidates while protecting little. Narrower tools — confidentiality backed by sound information security, client non-solicits for client-facing roles, garden leave for a few senior positions, deferred compensation that vests over time — may protect the same interests at lower cost. Counsel should confirm what is permissible in each state, and each country, where staff work.

retain.text: At-will employment is the U.S. default, limited by statutes, public policy, contracts and collective agreements; post-employment clauses carry much of the economic weight. Non-competes, non-solicits, confidentiality and invention assignment protect different interests and should be matched to them. Non-compete law is mainly state law and is changing; the FTC's 2024 rule never took effect. The best causal evidence shows reduced mobility, especially for specialists.

For each of these interests — client relationships, trade secrets, ownership of code — name the narrowest clause that protects it.

Non-compete law is mainly state law and changed in several states in 2025. The FTC’s 2024 rule was set aside in August 2024; the FTC dropped its appeals in September 2025 and removed the rule from the CFR in February 2026.
Quasi-experimental evidence (Michigan, 1985) shows reduced mobility, especially for specialists; survey evidence shows non-competes are common and rarely negotiated.

check.prompt: Which finding from Starr, Prescott and Bishara’s survey most directly challenges the claim that non-competes are freely bargained terms?

options.text: About 18 percent of labor force participants were bound by a non-compete.
Non-competes are more common in high-skill, high-pay jobs.
Only about 10 percent of workers reported negotiating over the clause, and roughly one-third were presented with it after accepting the job offer.

check.explanation: Bargaining requires negotiation and the ability to walk away. A low negotiation rate, and presentation after acceptance — when the worker may already have declined other offers — directly undercut the picture of a freely bargained term. The other findings describe prevalence and distribution, not the bargaining process.

optionFeedback.a: Prevalence says how common the clause is, not whether it was bargained over.
optionFeedback.b: Concentration in high-skill jobs is consistent with bargaining or with imposition; it does not distinguish them.
optionFeedback.d: Use in non-enforcing states raises questions about deterrence, but it is not direct evidence about bargaining.

check.prompt: An independent contractor writes software for a company under a signed agreement that says nothing about intellectual property. Under general U.S. copyright principles, who most likely owns the copyright in the code?

options.text: The company, because it paid for the work.

The contractor, because a contractor’s work is generally not a work made for hire absent a qualifying written agreement or assignment — though the company may have an implied right to use what it paid for.
The company and the contractor jointly, in equal shares.
No one, because software cannot be protected by copyright.

check.explanation: Works made for hire by default cover employees acting within the scope of their jobs. For independent contractors, ownership generally stays with the creator unless a signed writing assigns it or a qualifying work-for-hire agreement applies. Courts may find that the paying company has a license to use the work, which is why the missing clause matters.

optionFeedback.a: Payment alone does not transfer copyright from an independent contractor.
optionFeedback.c: Joint authorship requires specific conditions; payment and commissioning do not create it.
optionFeedback.d: Software code is protected by copyright as a literary work.

lessons.title: Agency, Fiduciary Duty and Institutional Constraints
lessons.summary: People who act for others — agents, officers, directors — owe duties of care and loyalty, and every organization operates inside institutional constraints that limit what any single agreement can do.
objectives: Explain actual and apparent authority and when an organization is bound by its agents.
Distinguish the duty of care from the duty of loyalty and explain how the business judgment rule shapes judicial review.
Recognize conflicts of interest and describe a sound process for handling them.
Describe how regulation, labor law, collective bargaining and league rules constrain organizational choices.
lessons.executive: When you act for an organization, you are its agent. You can bind it to contracts within your actual authority, and sometimes beyond it, if the other side reasonably relied on appearances the organization created. Directors and officers owe fiduciary duties: care, which courts judge mainly by the quality of the decision process rather than the outcome, and loyalty, which forbids putting personal interests ahead of the organization’s. The business judgment rule protects informed, disinterested, good-faith decisions even when they turn out badly; Smith v. Van Gorkom shows it does not protect uninformed ones. Above all of this sit institutional constraints — regulation, labor law and, in professional sports, collective bargaining agreements and league rules — that no single contract can override.

explore.text: **Educational material about general legal concepts — not legal advice. Consult a qualified attorney about any specific agreement.** Corporate and agency law is largely state law; the corporate-law examples below draw on Delaware, where many U.S. corporations are organized, and other states and countries differ.

In 1985 the Delaware Supreme Court held that the directors of a public company had breached their duty of care when they approved a cash-out merger. The price offered was a substantial premium over the market price of the stock, and no one accused the directors of self-dealing. The court's objection was to the process: the board had not informed itself of reasonably available information before agreeing to sell. Having acted on an uninformed basis, the directors lost the protection of the business judgment rule, and the case was sent back for a determination of damages.
Would you hold directors personally responsible for approving a sale at a premium to the market price? What would you have wanted them to do differently, and how would you know they had done enough?

The case, *Smith v. Van Gorkom*, is a fixture of corporate law courses because it teaches a counterintuitive point. Courts rarely second-guess the substance of business decisions, but they do examine whether the people making them did the work. Outcome is not the test; process is.

understand.title: Prerequisite: who owes duties to whom

blocks.text: A corporation is a legal person, separate from its owners. Shareholders elect a board of directors, which oversees the business and appoints officers who run it day to day. Directors and officers owe fiduciary duties to the corporation and, in the usual formulation, to its shareholders as a group. Employees and other representatives act as the organization's agents. Nonprofits, public agencies and member associations have analogous structures, with their own duties, oversight bodies and rules.

understand.text: Agency: when someone else's signature binds you

Agency law governs relationships in which one person, the **agent**, acts on behalf of another, the **principal**, and subject to its control. An agent's **actual authority** may be express — granted in words, such as a delegation-of-authority policy — or implied, meaning reasonably necessary to carry out an express grant. **Apparent authority** arises when the principal's own conduct leads a third party reasonably to believe the agent has authority: giving someone a title, letting them negotiate, honoring their past deals. A principal can be bound by a contract its agent made within apparent authority even if the agent exceeded internal limits.

Agents owe their principals duties of loyalty, obedience to lawful instructions, reasonable care and disclosure of relevant information. Employers are also generally liable for wrongs their employees commit within the scope of employment, a doctrine known as *respondeat superior*. Two lessons follow for any manager: know the limits of your own authority, and remember that people dealing with your organization may reasonably rely on what you appear able to do.
Fiduciary duties: care and loyalty

Directors and officers owe two core fiduciary duties. The **duty of care** requires them to act on an informed basis, considering the information reasonably available to them. *Van Gorkom* is the canonical example: the duty was breached by gross negligence in the decision process, not by a bad outcome. The **duty of loyalty** requires them to act in good faith in the organization's interest rather than their own. Self-dealing — standing on both sides of a transaction, taking for oneself an opportunity that belongs to the organization, or favoring a related party — is the classic loyalty problem.

The **business judgment rule** is a presumption that directors made an informed decision in good faith and in the honest belief that it served the company. A plaintiff must rebut the presumption, typically by showing that the directors were interested in the transaction, acted in bad faith or failed to inform themselves. If the presumption holds, courts will not substitute their judgment for the board's, however the decision turned out. *Van Gorkom* shows the other side: an uninformed decision forfeits that deference.

understand.caption: How courts tend to look at a board decision (simplified)
cells: Care problem: deference can be lost, as in Van Gorkom
Highest exposure: care and loyalty problems together
Business judgment rule: strong deference, even after a bad outcome
Loyalty problem: more searching review unless the conflict is disclosed and the decision made by disinterested people
understand.note: Teaching simplification of U.S., especially Delaware, corporate law. Standards of review, procedures for handling conflicts and limits on personal liability vary by jurisdiction and type of entity.

understand.text: Conflicts of interest are where most executives meet the duty of loyalty in practice. The standard process is simple to state and often skipped: disclose the interest fully and early, step away from the decision, let disinterested decision-makers evaluate it on the merits, and document what happened. A conflict handled this way is usually manageable. A conflict concealed and later discovered rarely is, because concealment converts a question about one transaction into a question about the person's integrity.
Institutions above the contract

Contracts and fiduciary duties operate inside a larger set of constraints. Regulators set rules that private agreements cannot waive, such as wage-and-hour, anti-discrimination, privacy and securities rules. Agencies are constrained too: the FTC's non-compete rule was set aside because a court found the agency lacked the authority to issue it. Labor law adds a further layer. Where employees are represented by a union, federal labor law generally requires the employer to bargain collectively over wages, hours and working conditions, and the resulting agreement sets terms that individual arrangements generally cannot undercut.

Professional sports leagues are a vivid case of institutional constraint. Clubs are members of a league whose constitution and rules bind them, and player employment terms are set within collective bargaining agreements negotiated between the clubs and the players' union, which typically address minimum salaries, standard contract forms, discipline and grievance arbitration. Baseball also has a distinctive antitrust history. In *Flood v. Kuhn* (1972) the Supreme Court left baseball's long-standing antitrust exemption in place and said any change was for Congress; the Curt Flood Act of 1998 then made the antitrust laws apply to matters directly relating to the employment of major league players, while the exemption's reach in other areas remains debated. For a leader inside such an organization, the practical point is that many questions that look like individual decisions — compensation, discipline, data use, scheduling — are already partly answered by agreements and rules negotiated elsewhere.

understand.title: Methodological note: why courts defer to business decisions

blocks.text: Courts give boards deference for reasons that echo earlier weeks. Judges are not business experts. Hindsight makes failed risks look reckless, a judgment bias of the kind Week 1 examines. And owners benefit when directors take sensible risks rather than avoid every decision that could be second-guessed. Process review is a compromise: a court cannot easily judge whether a decision was right, but it can judge whether the decision-makers were informed and disinterested.

The same logic applies inside organizations. Evaluating leaders by the quality of their decision process, not only by outcomes, is both fairer and more informative, because outcomes mix skill with luck. The hard part, in courtrooms and in performance reviews alike, is deciding how much information was “reasonably available” — a standard, in Lesson 1's terms, whose content is supplied after the fact.

challenge.text: Process review has costs. After decisions like *Van Gorkom*, boards learned to build records: longer meetings, outside advisers, written valuation opinions. Critics argue that some of this is defensive documentation that protects directors more than it improves decisions — a governance cousin of the measurement problems discussed in Week 8, in which the record of diligence becomes the target. Defenders reply that gathering information and hearing advisers does change decisions at the margin. Both can be true.

The business judgment rule is also criticized from the opposite direction, as too deferential. It can shield boards that approve risky strategies with thin oversight, and personal liability for directors is uncommon in practice because organizations commonly indemnify and insure their directors and, in some jurisdictions, may limit directors' personal liability for certain breaches. Deference that is right for honest mistakes can be wrong for persistent inattention.

Agency and fiduciary concepts also travel imperfectly. Nonprofit directors owe duties to a mission rather than to shareholders; public officials operate under ethics statutes and procurement rules; and civil-law jurisdictions, including most of Latin America, organize corporate and agency law differently from U.S. common law. When a decision crosses borders, treat the concepts in this lesson as a starting vocabulary, not as the governing law.

challenge.title: Executive twist: a conflict nobody asked about

blocks.text: You learn that a senior colleague on your organization's vendor-selection committee holds a small personal investment in one of the bidders. The colleague says it is immaterial and that raising it would embarrass everyone. Work through the sequence. Who has the authority to decide whether the interest is material — the colleague, you, or someone independent? What does the organization's conflict policy require, and who administers it? What is the cost of disclosure now compared with discovery after the contract is signed? Handling the conflict well is rarely about the size of the investment. It is about whether the decision process will remain defensible to people who were not in the room.

apply.text: Worked examples across sectors

**Technology.** A regional sales director signs a three-year reseller agreement with exclusive territory terms, although the company's delegation-of-authority policy requires the chief financial officer's approval for any exclusive arrangement. The reseller never saw the policy and dealt only with the director, whose title and past deals suggested authority. The company may be bound under apparent authority; its remedies against the director are internal. The lesson for leaders is to align titles, delegations and counterparties' reasonable expectations — and to tell key counterparties who can sign what. (Hypothetical.)

**Healthcare.** A hospital board considers a contract with an imaging company in which one trustee's family holds a stake. A sound process: the trustee discloses the interest in writing and leaves the room; the remaining trustees compare competing bids and an independent review of the terms; the minutes record the analysis. The same contract approved without disclosure would be vulnerable even if its terms were fair. (Hypothetical.)

**Government.** A program manager at a federal agency tells a contractor that additional funding will cover extra work. In U.S. federal contracting, only officials with delegated contracting authority can commit public funds, and the private-sector doctrine of apparent authority generally does not bind the government. A promise by someone without that authority may not bind the agency at all. Contractors who work with public bodies learn to ask who the authorized contracting officer is. (Hypothetical.)

Will the other side reasonably think I have authority?

Does anyone involved, including me, have a personal interest?
Undisclosed conflicts turn a business question into a loyalty question

Care is judged by process; the record should show the work

apply.text: In player development, leaders act as agents constantly: approving vendor quotes, signing facility agreements, making commitments to staff and to families of young players. The questions in the table apply directly. A promise to a staff member about a future role, a handshake agreement with a facility owner abroad, or a vendor arrangement with a company in which a colleague has an interest can each bind the organization or embarrass it. The discipline is the same as in any industry: know your authority, disclose interests early, document the process, and check whether a collective agreement, league rule or local law already decides the question.

retain.text: Organizations can be bound by agents acting within actual or apparent authority. Directors and officers owe care, judged mainly by process, and loyalty, which forbids self-dealing and requires conflicts to be handled openly. The business judgment rule protects informed, disinterested, good-faith decisions — not uninformed ones. Regulation, labor law, collective agreements and league rules set boundaries no individual contract can cross.

The duty of care is judged mainly by the quality of the decision process; the duty of loyalty forbids self-dealing and requires conflicts to be handled openly.

check.prompt: Which board is in the strongest position if shareholders later challenge the decision?

stimulus.text: Two fictional software companies each approve the acquisition of a smaller rival, and both acquisitions later lose money. Board A met three times over six weeks, reviewed financial projections and an outside adviser’s analysis, questioned management’s assumptions, and recorded its reasoning; no director had an interest in the target. Board B approved the deal in a single short meeting based on the chief executive’s oral summary, without written materials; one director, who did not disclose it, owned shares in the target.

options.text: Board B, because the deal was approved quickly and decisively.
Neither, because both deals lost money and courts judge boards by outcomes.
Board A, because an informed, disinterested process is what the business judgment rule protects, regardless of the outcome.
Both equally, because the business judgment rule protects all board decisions.

check.explanation: The business judgment rule presumes that directors acted on an informed basis, in good faith and without conflicts. Board A’s record supports that presumption even though the deal failed. Board B’s thin process raises a care problem of the Van Gorkom kind, and the undisclosed shareholding adds a loyalty problem.

optionFeedback.a: Speed is not the test; a quick, uninformed decision is exactly what can forfeit deference.
optionFeedback.b: Courts generally do not judge boards by outcomes; they examine process and conflicts.
optionFeedback.d: The presumption can be rebutted by showing a lack of information or a conflict, both present for Board B.

check.prompt: A company whose warehouse employees are represented by a union wants to change overtime pay by asking each employee to sign an individual agreement. Which institutional constraint is most directly relevant?

The duty to bargain collectively with the union over wages and working conditions, and the existing collective bargaining agreement, which individual agreements generally cannot undercut.
Promissory estoppel, because employees relied on the old overtime rules.
At-will employment, which allows the employer to change any term at any time.

check.explanation: Where employees are represented, federal labor law generally requires the employer to bargain with the union over wages, hours and working conditions, and terms set by the collective agreement govern. Going around the union with individual agreements runs into that constraint, whatever the merits of the change.

optionFeedback.a: The business judgment rule concerns judicial deference to boards in disputes with shareholders, not labor-law obligations.
optionFeedback.c: Reliance doctrines are not the primary constraint when a collective agreement and a statutory duty to bargain apply.
optionFeedback.d: Represented employees are typically covered by just-cause and bargaining protections that displace at-will flexibility.
