lessons.title: Working With Counsel: Timing, Privilege and Legal Risk
lessons.summary: Using lawyers well means involving them at the right moment, protecting privileged communications, asking questions that produce forecasts, and owning the business judgment that remains.
objectives: Identify situations that warrant involving counsel early and those that do not.
Explain the basics of attorney-client privilege and work product in an organization, including how protection is lost.
Frame questions for counsel that produce usable, probabilistic advice.
Integrate a legal forecast into a business decision without delegating the decision to counsel.
lessons.executive: Executives misuse lawyers in two opposite ways: too late, after facts and documents have hardened, and too broadly, by copying counsel on everything in the hope of making it privileged. Privilege protects confidential communications made to obtain legal advice. In an organization the client is the entity, and the Supreme Court’s Upjohn decision extends protection to employees who give counsel the facts needed for that advice. Privilege is easily waived by sharing outside the circle, and it never covers the underlying facts or ordinary business advice. Bring counsel in when stakes are high, actions are irreversible or the law is unfamiliar; ask for forecasts with ranges and assumptions; and keep the business decision yours.

explore.text: **Educational material about general legal concepts — not legal advice. Consult a qualified attorney about any specific agreement.** Privilege and professional-responsibility rules vary across U.S. jurisdictions and differ substantially in other countries; this lesson describes general U.S. concepts only.

A manager at a software company receives a complaint from an employee alleging that a team lead made discriminatory comments. The manager emails the company's employment lawyer, describes the facts and asks how to proceed. The lawyer replies with advice. Wanting to be transparent, the manager forwards the reply to the outside recruiting firm that placed the team lead, and later summarizes it in a team chat channel. (Hypothetical.)

Before reading on: which of these communications are likely to be protected from disclosure if the complaint becomes a lawsuit, and which are not? What might the manager's transparency have cost the company?

The manager acted in good faith and may still have weakened the company's ability to keep its legal advice confidential. Privilege rules are not intuitive, and the moment to learn them is before a crisis, not during one. This lesson covers when to call a lawyer, what privilege protects, how to brief counsel, and how to turn a legal forecast into a decision.

blocks.text: When a lawyer works for an organization, whether in-house or as outside counsel, the client is normally the organization itself, acting through its authorized representatives. The lawyer does not represent you personally, even if you are the person who called. If your interests and the organization's diverge — for example, if your own conduct is under review — the organization's lawyer cannot advise you about your personal position, and you may need your own counsel. Organizational lawyers often say this explicitly at the start of an internal interview.

understand.text: Attorney-client privilege and work product

The **attorney-client privilege** protects confidential communications between a client and its lawyer made for the purpose of obtaining or giving legal advice. In *Upjohn Co. v. United States* (1981), the Supreme Court considered an internal investigation in which a company's general counsel had sent questionnaires to managers and interviewed employees about questionable payments abroad. The Court rejected a narrow test that would have protected only communications from the small “control group” of senior executives, reasoning that lawyers need information from employees throughout an organization to give sound advice. Communications from employees to corporate counsel, made at the direction of superiors to secure legal advice for the company, can be privileged.

The Court stressed that the privilege protects communications, not facts: a witness can still be asked what happened, even if the same facts were reported to counsel. It also held that the **work-product doctrine** applied to the tax summons in that case. Work product protects materials prepared in anticipation of litigation, such as a lawyer's interview notes and analysis, with especially strong protection for the lawyer's mental impressions and opinions.

After *Upjohn*, lawyers conducting internal interviews commonly give what practitioners call an *Upjohn warning*: the lawyer represents the company, not the employee; the conversation is privileged, but the privilege belongs to the company, which may decide to waive it and share what the employee said with regulators or others.

understand.caption: What privilege generally does and does not cover
rows: A confidential email to counsel asking for legal advice about a termination
The underlying facts of the termination, which must be disclosed if relevant
The same advice forwarded to an outside vendor or posted in a team channel
Notes of counsel's interviews in an internal investigation
Business advice that happens to come from a lawyer
Analysis prepared by counsel in anticipation of litigation
Ordinary business documents later sent to counsel
A meeting held to obtain legal advice, attended only by people who need to be there
A routine business meeting at which a lawyer happens to be present
understand.note: General U.S. teaching summary. Privilege rules vary by jurisdiction and context, for example in regulatory investigations and cross-border matters.

understand.text: Three habits protect privilege better than any label. Keep legal-advice communications to the people who need them. Separate legal questions from business discussion rather than mixing them in one thread. And do not forward or summarize counsel's advice outside that circle without asking first. Writing “privileged and confidential” at the top of a document does not make it privileged if it is not, in substance, a confidential request for or provision of legal advice.
When to call a lawyer

understand.caption: When to involve counsel (a practitioner heuristic)
cells: Use templates and policies; escalate if the facts change
A brief consultation: one short question can prevent a costly precedent
Involve counsel in review; standard terms can hide large exposures
Involve counsel early, before documents, commitments or public statements harden
understand.note: Practitioner heuristic, not a legal standard. Some situations warrant counsel regardless of the grid: threatened litigation, government inquiries, allegations of discrimination, harassment or fraud, data breaches, and anything involving personal liability.

understand.text: Preservation deserves emphasis. Once a dispute or investigation is reasonably anticipated, organizations are generally expected to preserve relevant documents and data, including messages on phones and collaboration tools. Routine deletion that is harmless on an ordinary day can look like destruction of evidence on the wrong day. Counsel usually issues a formal *litigation hold*; executives should stop deleting relevant material without waiting for one.

steps.label: Pause
steps.text: Avoid statements, admissions and hasty new documents.

steps.label: Preserve
steps.text: Keep relevant records; do not delete or edit.

steps.label: Call
steps.text: Contact counsel through the organization’s channel.

steps.label: Brief
steps.text: Facts known and unknown, documents, deadlines, the business objective.

steps.label: Decide
steps.text: Combine counsel’s forecast with business judgment.

steps.label: Record
steps.text: Document the decision and its basis appropriately.

understand.text: Asking questions that produce useful answers

items: What question are you answering, under which jurisdiction's law, and on what assumed facts?
What is your best estimate of the outcome, and what range would not surprise you?
Which fact, if it turned out differently, would change your view most?
What would it cost, in money and time, to get a more certain answer?
What are our options, including doing nothing, and what is the legal risk of each?
What should we not do or say while this is pending?
Is this legal advice, business advice or both — and should we keep them in separate communications?

understand.title: Methodological note: legal forecasts are forecasts

blocks.text: A recurring theme of Week 1 is that confidence and accuracy can come apart, especially when feedback is slow and outcomes are noisy. Litigation fits that description: cases take years, most settle, and lawyers rarely learn how their early estimates compared with final outcomes. It is a reasonable hypothesis — not a finding established in this course — that legal outcome predictions share the calibration problems of other expert forecasts.

The practical implications are modest and cheap. Ask for ranges and reasons rather than a single number. When stakes are high, compare two independent views. And keep a simple record of predictions and outcomes for your organization's legal matters, so that over time you learn which kinds of forecasts deserve confidence. The Strategic Decision Journal can hold these entries.

challenge.text: Lawyers' incentives are not identical to the organization's. Outside counsel bills for time; in-house counsel is more often blamed for legal problems than for missed opportunities. Both pressures can push advice toward caution. That is not a reason to discount legal advice. It is a reason to ask what a risk-neutral view would be, what the realistic worst case is, and what excessive caution would cost.

Over-lawyering has costs too. Routing every decision through counsel slows organizations, teaches managers to avoid judgment and can turn a legal department into a “department of no.” Copying lawyers on routine emails in the hope of creating privilege usually fails and can damage credibility with a court when the practice is exposed. The skill is calibration: recognizing the decisions in which the law actually changes the answer.

Holmes's prediction view cuts both ways. If law is what courts will do, legal risk is a probability distribution, and some legal risks are worth taking: a contract term that might not be enforced, a novel product that might attract scrutiny. Deciding which risks to take is a business and ethical judgment informed by counsel, not one counsel can make alone. Week 13 examines the ethical side of that choice.

Finally, the U.S. model does not travel well. Many countries treat communications with in-house lawyers differently from those with outside lawyers, and some protect them less. In cross-border matters, ask local counsel how privilege works before anyone writes anything down.

apply.text: Worked example: a briefing note to counsel

A regional hospital's chief operating officer learns that a departing physician group intends to open a competing clinic nearby and has begun contacting patients. The group's agreement contains a non-compete and a patient non-solicitation clause. Before calling outside counsel, the COO writes a one-page briefing note: the facts known and unknown; the relevant documents (the agreement, the group's notice of departure, reports of patient contacts); the deadlines; the hospital's business objective, which is continuity of patient care and referral relationships rather than punishing the physicians; and three questions — whether the restrictive covenants are likely to be enforceable under the state's law for physicians, what the hospital may say to patients, and what it should preserve now. (Hypothetical.)

The note does three things. It saves billable time. It makes counsel's assumptions visible. And it states the business objective, which allows counsel to say that the legally strongest move, such as seeking an injunction, may not be the commercially best one. A well-briefed lawyer can give a better forecast faster.

In professional baseball and other sports organizations, legal questions cluster around people and information: staff hiring and departures, workplace complaints and discipline, data and privacy, vendor and facility agreements, and international operations where local law, immigration rules and league regulations all apply. A department leader's role is usually not to answer those questions but to notice them early, keep facts and documents intact, route them through the organization's legal function, and translate counsel's forecast into an operational decision. In international settings, assume that U.S. concepts such as at-will employment or attorney-client privilege may not exist in the same form, and ask local counsel rather than extrapolate.

retain.text: Organizational counsel represents the entity. Privilege protects confidential communications made to obtain legal advice — including, after *Upjohn*, employees' communications to counsel — but not facts or business advice, and sharing outside the circle can waive it. Call counsel early when stakes are high or actions irreversible, preserve records once a dispute is anticipated, brief counsel concisely, and ask for forecasts with ranges. The decision remains yours.
Name two ways a manager can unintentionally waive privilege, and one habit that prevents each.
What did Upjohn decide about which employees' communications with counsel can be privileged, and why?
Write the three questions you would most want answered before acting on a lawyer's “60 percent” estimate.

takeaways: Organizational counsel represents the entity, not you; Upjohn protects employees’ communications to counsel made to secure legal advice for the company.
Privilege covers confidential legal-advice communications, not underlying facts or business advice, and is easily waived by sharing outside the circle.
Involve counsel early when stakes are high or actions irreversible; preserve records as soon as a dispute is anticipated.
Ask counsel for forecasts with ranges and assumptions; the business decision remains yours.

check.prompt: Which of the following actions by a manager are most likely to put the confidentiality of counsel’s legal advice at risk? Select all that apply.

options.text: Forwarding counsel’s advice email to an outside consultant who is not working with counsel.
Asking counsel a follow-up question by replying only to counsel.
Summarizing counsel’s advice in a company-wide chat channel.
Sharing counsel’s advice with the two colleagues responsible for carrying it out, as counsel suggested.
Posting counsel’s analysis on a public industry forum to show the company is careful.

check.explanation: Privilege depends on confidentiality. Sharing advice with outsiders or broadly inside the organization, beyond the people who need it, risks waiver. Replying to counsel or sharing with the people who must act on the advice, at counsel’s direction, generally keeps it within the circle.

optionFeedback.a: Correct: an outsider not working with counsel breaks confidentiality.
optionFeedback.b: Not a risk: a reply to counsel seeking legal advice is itself a privileged communication.
optionFeedback.c: Correct: broad internal distribution beyond those who need the advice can undermine confidentiality.
optionFeedback.d: Generally not a risk: sharing with those who need the advice to act on it, as counsel directs, stays within the circle.

check.prompt: At the start of an internal interview, the company’s lawyer tells an employee: “I represent the company, not you. This conversation is privileged, but the privilege belongs to the company.” What follows?

options.text: The employee can prevent the company from ever sharing what was said.
The company may decide to waive the privilege and disclose what the employee said, for example to a regulator.
Nothing the employee says can be used by the company for any purpose.
The lawyer must keep the employee’s statements confidential from the company’s leadership.

check.explanation: This is the familiar Upjohn warning. Because the organization is the client, it controls the privilege and may waive it. The employee is not the client and cannot block disclosure, which is why employees whose personal interests are at stake may need their own counsel.

optionFeedback.a: The privilege belongs to the company; the employee cannot control it.
optionFeedback.c: The company can use the information to obtain legal advice and make decisions; privilege limits disclosure to outsiders, not use by the client.
optionFeedback.d: The lawyer’s client is the company, so the lawyer reports to the company, not around it.

glossary.definition: A teaching and writing structure — Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion — for organizing legal analysis. A heuristic for disciplined thinking, not a theory of how judges decide.
Identifying the legal and commercial questions that a set of facts or a document raises, before attempting to answer them.
A rule fixes the content of a command before people act (“within 30 days”); a standard leaves the content to be supplied afterward by a decision-maker (“within a reasonable time”).
The practice of following earlier decisions of higher courts in the same jurisdiction on materially similar questions; decisions from other jurisdictions are persuasive only.

Which party must persuade the decision-maker, and to what standard: preponderance of the evidence in most civil cases, beyond a reasonable doubt in criminal cases, and clear and convincing evidence for some civil claims.
What each party gives in a bargained-for exchange — a promise or performance sought in return for the other side’s — required for most contracts to be enforceable.
A doctrine under which a promise may be enforced without consideration when the promisor should have expected reliance, the promisee did rely, and injustice can be avoided only by enforcement.
The interpretive principle that genuinely ambiguous contract language is construed against the party that drafted it, usually as a tie-breaker of last resort.
An event that must occur before a party’s duty to perform arises. If it does not occur, the duty never becomes due and there is no breach.
A representation is a statement of fact made to induce a contract; a warranty is a promise that a stated fact is true, backed by a remedy. Commercial contracts often combine them.
A promise by one party to cover specified losses or claims suffered by the other, often including the cost of defending claims brought by third parties.
Money that puts the injured party where it would have been had the contract been performed, limited by foreseeability, reasonable certainty and the duty to mitigate.
The U.S. default under which either party may end employment at any time for any lawful reason, subject to statutory, public-policy, contractual and collective-bargaining limits.

A clause restricting a worker from working for, or starting, a competing business for a period and area after leaving; enforceability depends mainly on state law. Non-solicitation clauses, by contrast, bar soliciting clients or employees.
A clause transferring to an employer or client ownership of inventions and work product; its wording determines whether personal or pre-existing work is captured.

Authority a third party reasonably believes an agent has because of the principal’s own conduct, such as a title or a history of honored deals; it can bind the principal even if internal limits were exceeded.
The duties of care and loyalty owed by those who act for others — directors, officers, agents — to decide on an informed basis and to put the principal’s interests ahead of their own.
A presumption that directors made an informed decision in good faith and without conflicts. If it holds, courts do not second-guess the merits of the decision.
Protection from disclosure for confidential communications between a client and its lawyer made to obtain or give legal advice. It covers communications, not facts, and can be waived by sharing.
Protection for materials prepared in anticipation of litigation, such as a lawyer’s notes and analysis, with especially strong protection for the lawyer’s opinions and mental impressions.

exercise.title: Contract Lab

intro.text: **Educational exercise on a fictional document — not legal advice.** The agreement, the company and the consultant are invented for teaching, and nothing here evaluates any real agreement. Educational material about general legal concepts — not legal advice. Consult a qualified attorney about any specific agreement.

You are reviewing a draft Independent Consulting Agreement that a fictional software company, Tessaline Analytics, Inc., has sent to an independent consultant, Mara Ilunga, who would advise it on demand-forecasting models. Read it as a careful business reader preparing to brief counsel. Flag each clause that raises a legal or commercial issue, choose the category that best describes the main issue, and add a short note on why it matters and what you would ask. Some clauses are unremarkable. Read from the consultant's side, but notice where a term also creates risk for the company that drafted it.

items: One-sided terms: a right for one party and a duty for the other.
Standards with no benchmark: “reasonable,” “satisfactory,” “in Company's judgment,” “sole discretion.”
Clauses whose effect depends on another clause — for example, assignment and the restrictive covenants, or the entire-agreement clause and earlier promises.
Duration: what survives the end of the agreement, and for how long.
What is missing as well as what is present.

intro.text: Scoring compares your flags with the author's key: issues found, issues missed, and flags with no matching issue. The key is one informed reading, not the only defensible one; a lawyer applying a particular state's law might weight the issues differently. Spend about 20 minutes flagging and 15 minutes reviewing the explanations.

document.title: Independent Consulting Agreement (fictional)
document.parties: Tessaline Analytics, Inc. (“Company”) and Mara Ilunga (“Consultant”). Fictional draft prepared for teaching, dated March 2, 2026.

clauses.heading: 1. Purpose
clauses.text: Company wishes to engage Consultant, an independent consultant, to advise on demand-forecasting models as described in Consultant's proposal dated February 10, 2026 (the “Proposal”). Consultant wishes to provide those services on the terms below.

clauses.heading: 2. Services
clauses.text: Consultant will provide forecasting advisory services and such other services as Company may request from time to time (the “Services”). Consultant will deliver a written report each month summarizing the work performed.

clauses.heading: 3. Time Commitment and Relationship
clauses.text: Consultant will be available to Company from 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. on business days, will use Company-issued equipment, and will not provide services to any other business during the Term. Consultant is an independent contractor and is solely responsible for all taxes, insurance and benefits.

clauses.heading: 4. Fees and Payment
clauses.text: Company will pay Consultant $18,000 per month. Each monthly payment is due within 60 days after Company accepts the corresponding monthly report. Acceptance is in Company's sole discretion.

clauses.heading: 5. Expenses
clauses.text: Company will reimburse reasonable travel expenses that Company has approved in writing in advance, within 30 days after Consultant submits receipts.

clauses.heading: 6. Intellectual Property
clauses.text: All work product, inventions, ideas, software, methods and know-how that Consultant creates or conceives during the Term, whether or not related to the Services and whether or not created using Company resources, are the sole property of Company. Consultant assigns to Company all right, title and interest in them, including in any pre-existing materials Consultant uses in performing the Services.

clauses.heading: 7. Confidentiality
clauses.text: Consultant will hold in confidence, in perpetuity, all information Consultant learns in connection with this Agreement, and will not use it for any purpose other than the Services.

clauses.heading: 8. Restrictive Covenants
clauses.text: During the Term and for 24 months afterward, Consultant will not, anywhere in the world, provide services to any business that competes with Company or any of its affiliates, and will not solicit or accept work from any client or prospective client of Company.

clauses.heading: 9. Term and Termination
clauses.text: This Agreement runs for 12 months. Company may terminate it at any time, for any reason, on five days' written notice. Consultant may terminate only if Company materially breaches this Agreement and fails to cure within 90 days after written notice. On any termination, Company owes no fees for any report it has not accepted.

clauses.heading: 10. Warranties
clauses.text: Consultant warrants that all work product will be accurate, complete, free of errors and fit for any purpose for which Company chooses to use it.

clauses.heading: 11. Indemnification
clauses.text: Consultant will defend, indemnify and hold harmless Company, its affiliates and their officers and employees from any and all claims, losses and expenses arising out of or relating to the Services or this Agreement, regardless of cause.

clauses.heading: 12. Limitation of Liability
clauses.text: Company's total liability under this Agreement will not exceed the fees paid to Consultant in the one month before the claim arose. Company will not be liable for any indirect or consequential damages.

clauses.heading: 13. Non-Disparagement
clauses.text: Consultant will not at any time make any statement, in any medium, that could reflect negatively on Company, its affiliates, products, officers or employees.

clauses.heading: 14. Conduct
clauses.text: Company may terminate this Agreement immediately, and withhold any unpaid fees, if Consultant engages in any conduct that, in Company's judgment, brings Consultant or Company into public disrepute.

clauses.heading: 15. Assignment; Entire Agreement
clauses.text: Company may assign this Agreement, including Sections 6 through 8, to any affiliate or successor without Consultant's consent. Consultant may not assign or subcontract. This Agreement is the entire agreement between the parties and supersedes all prior proposals, discussions and understandings, including the Proposal.

clauses.heading: 16. Governing Law and Disputes
clauses.text: This Agreement is governed by the law of the state in which Company's headquarters is located, without regard to conflict-of-laws principles. Any dispute will be resolved exclusively in the courts of the county in which Company's headquarters is located. Consultant waives trial by jury. Company is entitled to recover its attorneys' fees in any action to enforce this Agreement.

categories.label: Risk allocation: warranties, indemnity, liability caps

issues.explanation: “Such other services as Company may request” has no boundary, while the fee is fixed. Combined with Section 15, which supersedes the Proposal that described the work, Consultant could be asked to do almost anything for the same fee, and any limits she negotiated in the Proposal disappear.
issues.ask: Can the Services be defined in an attached statement of work, with a written change-order process and additional fees for work outside it?

issues.explanation: Company sets fixed hours, supplies equipment and bars other clients — features associated with employment — while labelling Consultant an independent contractor responsible for her own taxes, insurance and benefits. That mismatch creates classification risk for Company under tax and employment rules (whose tests differ by agency and state) and gives Consultant exclusivity without employee protections.
issues.ask: Which classification tests apply, and can the engagement be restructured around deliverables, with Consultant controlling her hours and free to serve non-competing clients?

issues.explanation: Payment depends on acceptance in Company's sole discretion, with no criteria, no deadline and no deemed acceptance, followed by a further 60 days. Company can delay payment indefinitely without obviously breaching. Courts sometimes read a duty of good faith into such discretion, but relying on that means litigation, not a payment term.
issues.ask: Will Company agree to objective acceptance criteria, deemed acceptance if no written objection is given within ten business days, and payment 30 days after invoice?

issues.explanation: The assignment reaches everything Consultant conceives during the Term, related or not, and even her pre-existing materials. For an independent consultant with other work and her own tools, that transfers assets Company has not paid for and invites ownership disputes. Because a contractor generally owns copyright in her work unless she assigns it in writing, the scope of this clause decides who owns what.
issues.ask: Can the assignment be limited to deliverables created for Company under this Agreement, with Consultant keeping pre-existing materials and general know-how and granting Company a license to any pre-existing materials built into the deliverables?

issues.explanation: Perpetual confidentiality may suit genuine trade secrets but not all information. The clause lacks the standard exclusions — information that is public, already known to Consultant, independently developed or received from a third party without restriction — and has no carve-out for disclosures required by law or court order.
issues.ask: Can we add the standard exclusions and a compelled-disclosure carve-out, keep perpetual protection for trade secrets, and set a fixed term for other information?

issues.explanation: Twenty-four months, worldwide, covering any business that competes with Company or any affiliate, plus a bar on accepting work from prospective clients. For an independent consultant this could foreclose her livelihood. Enforceability of non-competes varies sharply by state, and some states refuse to enforce most of them, but even an unenforceable clause can deter clients. Section 15 magnifies the reach by letting Company assign the covenant to affiliates and successors.
issues.ask: Under the governing law and where Consultant works, is this enforceable at all? Would Company accept a non-solicitation limited to clients Consultant actually served, for a shorter period, in place of the non-compete?

issues.explanation: Company can exit on five days' notice for any reason; Consultant can exit only after a 90-day cure period following a material breach. And no fees are owed for unaccepted reports, so termination can erase payment for work already performed.
issues.ask: Can termination rights be mutual — for example, 30 days' notice for either party — with payment for all work performed through the termination date?

issues.explanation: Advisory forecasting work cannot be guaranteed error-free and “fit for any purpose” Company chooses. The warranty turns advice into an outcome guarantee and creates liability for any downstream use, including uses Consultant never knew about.
issues.ask: Will Company accept a warranty that the Services will be performed in a professional manner consistent with generally accepted industry standards, with re-performance as the primary remedy and other warranties disclaimed?

issues.explanation: Indemnity for “any and all claims … regardless of cause” would make Consultant pay for losses caused by Company's own negligence or misuse of her work, including the cost of defending claims from the start. It is one-way and uncapped.
issues.ask: Can indemnity be limited to third-party claims caused by Consultant's negligence, willful misconduct or infringement, made mutual, and capped?

issues.explanation: Company's liability is capped at one month's fees and excludes consequential damages; Consultant's liability is not capped at all, and Section 11 expands it. Company risks almost nothing; Consultant's exposure is unlimited.
issues.ask: Can the cap and the consequential-damages exclusion apply to both parties — for example, total fees paid or payable — with any carve-outs also mutual?

issues.explanation: Perpetual and one-way; “could reflect negatively” would reach truthful statements, ordinary professional criticism and possibly testimony, and it may conflict with laws that protect certain disclosures, such as reports to government agencies. There is no reciprocal obligation on Company.
issues.ask: Can it be mutual, time-limited, limited to knowingly false statements, and carve out truthful statements required by law or made to regulators?

issues.explanation: “Public disrepute” in Company's judgment is undefined and discretionary, and it triggers both immediate termination and forfeiture of fees already earned. A morals clause this vague lets Company exit and avoid payment on a contested reading.
issues.ask: Can the trigger be defined objectively (for example, conviction of a serious crime or proven fraud), and can fees for work already performed be paid in any event?

issues.explanation: Two quiet provisions. Company may assign the Agreement, including the IP and restrictive covenants, to any affiliate or successor, so the non-compete could end up protecting an acquirer's unrelated businesses. And the entire-agreement clause supersedes the Proposal, erasing any limits on scope, hours or rates it contained.
issues.ask: Can assignment require consent, or at least limit the restrictive covenants to the original business, and can the Proposal be attached as an exhibit that governs scope?

issues.explanation: Exclusive venue in Company's home county, a jury waiver and one-way attorneys' fees raise the cost of any claim Consultant might bring, especially for unpaid fees, while lowering Company's. The choice of law may also decide whether the restrictive covenants are enforceable.
issues.ask: Can fees go to the prevailing party, can venue be neutral or where Consultant works, and should counsel check whether the chosen law can govern restrictive covenants for someone who lives and works in another state?

config.disclaimer: Educational exercise on a fictional document — not legal advice. Consult a qualified attorney about any specific agreement.

debrief.text: What the lab shows. Most of the seeded issues follow three patterns. One-sided rights: termination, liability caps, attorneys' fees, assignment. Open standards controlled by one party: scope, acceptance, conduct. And reach beyond the bargain: intellectual property, confidentiality, restrictive covenants, non-disparagement. Recognizing the pattern is faster and more reliable than memorizing clause types, and it transfers to agreements you have never seen.

What the lab does not show. It does not tell you whether any clause is enforceable. That depends on the governing law and the facts, and — for restrictive covenants and worker classification especially — on statutes and decisions that vary by state and change over time. The lab trains the first pass: what to flag, why it matters, what to ask. That is exactly the material a lawyer can use efficiently.

Prioritization matters as much as detection. In a negotiation (Week 7), the consultant will not win every point. Terms that create unbounded exposure — the indemnity, the uncapped liability, the IP overreach, the payment discretion — deserve more attention than irritants such as venue or the wording of the non-disparagement clause. A good memo ranks.

A department leader who engages outside experts sees this document from the other side. An agreement this one-sided may deter the best consultants, raise prices, slow the engagement and create classification and enforceability risk for the organization that drafted it. Fair, clear terms are often the cheaper risk control.

assumptions: The document is fictional and simplified; real agreements include definitions, schedules and further terms.
The key reflects general U.S. contract concepts; the governing state's law can change both the legal effect and the severity of an issue.
Severity ratings (high, medium) are the author's judgment from the consultant's perspective and are teaching heuristics, not legal assessments.
A flag counts as a match when its clause and category match a key issue; other reasonable categorizations exist, so review the explanations for near-misses.
Clauses 1 and 5 are seeded without issues; reasonable readers may still note minor points about them.

case.title: The Contract Problem
case.fiction: All people, organizations and data in this case are fictional. The case is an educational exercise about general legal and commercial concepts — not legal advice. Consult a qualified attorney about any specific agreement.

body.text: Five business days

The offer arrived on a Tuesday evening, as a forty-one-page PDF attached to a two-line email. Nadia Ferro read the first page three times. Orrisbane Robotics, a privately held warehouse-automation company with about 900 employees, wanted her as Vice President of Applied AI. The base salary was 24 percent above what she earned now. There was a sign-on bonus large enough to clear her remaining student loans, a grant of restricted stock units the recruiter described as “life-changing if the company goes public,” and a role she had wanted for a decade: build an applied research group from scratch and report directly to the chief executive.
The email's second line said the offer would expire at 5 p.m. the following Tuesday. Five business days.

Nadia, 41, was director of machine-learning platforms at Pellucid Freight Systems, a logistics software company of roughly 3,000 people. She had been there seven years, had built the team that ran its forecasting models, and was respected and a little restless. Pellucid was in the middle of a reorganization. Her manager had hinted at a promotion “once the dust settles,” which, Nadia had learned, could mean six months or never.
The fine print
On Wednesday morning, before work, she read the whole agreement with a legal pad beside her. By the time she finished, the pad held eleven notes. Several worried her more than she expected.

The duties clause said she would perform “such duties as the Chief Executive Officer may assign from time to time, including leadership of any business unit of the Company or its affiliates.” The CEO, Elias Brandt, had spent forty minutes on a video call describing the research group she would build. None of that description appeared in the document. Another clause allowed Orrisbane to “reassign Executive to any affiliate,” and Orrisbane had a manufacturing affiliate overseas.

The restrictive covenants ran for eighteen months after departure and covered “any business that develops, deploys or advises on artificial intelligence, robotics or automation products, anywhere in the world,” plus a 24-month ban on soliciting any Orrisbane employee or customer. Nadia did the arithmetic on her own career. Almost every company that might hire her next would fall inside that definition.

The invention-assignment clause transferred to Orrisbane “all inventions, works and ideas conceived or reduced to practice during employment, whether or not during working hours or using Company resources,” and added that she assigned “all right, title and interest in any pre-existing intellectual property incorporated into Company products.” For eight years Nadia had maintained an open-source library for route optimization. It had a few thousand users, a small community of contributors, and a modest following among logistics engineers. It was, she realized, exactly the kind of tool a warehouse-robotics company might want to build into its products. She also taught an evening course at a community college and had half-written a textbook.

The compensation terms had their own catches. The sign-on bonus was repayable in full if she resigned “for any reason” or was terminated “for Cause” within 24 months. “Cause” was defined to include “failure to perform Executive's duties to the reasonable satisfaction of the Chief Executive Officer” and “conduct that, in the Board's judgment, is detrimental to the Company's reputation.” A termination for cause also forfeited all unvested stock units and eliminated severance. Severance without cause was three months' base salary, conditioned on signing a release that included a permanent non-disparagement obligation. The annual bonus target was 30 percent of salary, payable “at the Company's sole discretion.” Disputes would go to mandatory arbitration in Orrisbane's home city, except that Orrisbane could go to court to enforce the restrictive covenants. The governing-law clause selected the law of Orrisbane's home state. Nadia would work remotely from the state where she lived, which was not the same state.
Three conversations

On Wednesday afternoon Nadia called the recruiter, Simone Achterberg, and asked whether the terms were negotiable. Simone was warm and practiced. “These are the company's standard executive terms,” she said. “Honestly, nobody negotiates them. Elias is very excited about you, and I would hate for this to turn into a back-and-forth.” When Nadia asked whether the deadline could move, Simone said she would “check,” and did not call back.

On Thursday, Elias Brandt called her himself. He was charismatic and direct. He told her the research group would have a budget of “a few million a year” and that she would hire her own team. When she raised the non-compete, he laughed. “We've never enforced one of those against anyone who left on good terms,” he said. “It's there for the bad actors. You're not a bad actor.” When she mentioned her open-source library, he said, “Of course you keep that — that's your thing.” She wrote both statements down. Later that evening she noticed the clause on page thirty-eight: the agreement was “the entire agreement between the parties and supersedes all prior discussions and representations.”

On Friday she had dinner with her friend Tomás Reyes, a commercial real-estate lawyer. He skimmed the non-compete on her phone and shrugged. “Non-competes are basically dead after the FTC banned them,” he said. “I wouldn't lose sleep.” Nadia had read enough news to doubt that, but not enough to know what was true now. Tomás gave her the name of an employment lawyer, Grace Okonjo, who reviewed executive agreements. Grace's assistant said Grace could meet the following Wednesday — the day after the offer expired — and quoted a flat fee of $3,500 for review and a negotiation memo.
The counteroffer

Over the weekend, word reached Pellucid. On Monday morning Nadia's manager offered a 10 percent raise, a retention bonus paid over two years, and a written commitment to a vice-president title at the next promotion cycle. Pellucid's offer came with a simple one-page letter. Her existing agreement with Pellucid had a 12-month restriction on soliciting Pellucid employees — which mattered, because two of her best engineers had already asked whether they could follow her to Orrisbane.

Nadia's spouse, an epidemiologist with a stable job, was supportive and practical. “I don't care which job you take,” he said. “I care that you don't sign something you'll spend two years regretting.”
Monday night

By Monday night Nadia had a spreadsheet, a legal pad full of notes and a draft email to Simone that she had rewritten four times. She saw several paths. She could sign by the deadline and trust the CEO. She could sign while asking for two or three changes and accept whatever came back. She could ask for a one-week extension so Grace could review the agreement, at the risk of signaling that she would be difficult. She could send a full list of requested changes. Or she could take Pellucid's offer, which paid less and carried fewer restrictions, and wait for a better opportunity.

She did not know whether the non-compete would be enforceable where she lived, or under the law Orrisbane had chosen. She did not know whether Orrisbane had ever negotiated these terms with anyone else. She did not know what her stock units would be worth, or whether the company would go public at all. She did know that the offer expired in less than twenty-four hours.
