questions: Rank the issues in Orrisbane’s agreement by their importance to Nadia. Which two would you treat as must-haves, which as tradeable, and which would you accept as written? State the criteria behind your ranking.

What weight should Nadia give to the CEO’s oral assurances and to her friend’s claim that non-competes are “dead”? What would she need to find out, and from whom, to replace both with something reliable?
Draft three questions Nadia should put to an employment lawyer and two she should put to Orrisbane directly. Why does the audience change the question?
Take Orrisbane’s side. Which of these terms protect legitimate interests, and which risk losing the candidate or creating legal exposure? What would a well-advised company change?
Is signing by the deadline and “sorting it out later” ever a defensible choice here? Under what conditions?

perspectives.title: Negotiate the few terms that matter most, then sign
perspectives.text: The opportunity is real and the deadline is pressing. Nadia should ask for a short extension and, whether or not she gets it, request a focused set of changes in writing: an excluded-projects schedule naming the open-source library and textbook; an objective definition of cause; a pro-rated sign-on repayment that does not apply if she is terminated without cause; and a narrower non-compete limited to warehouse-automation competitors, or replaced by a customer non-solicit. A short, reasoned list signals professionalism, not difficulty, and the response will reveal how Orrisbane treats disagreements.

perspectives.title: Pause until qualified counsel has reviewed it
perspectives.text: The deadline is a negotiating device, and a company that will not wait one week for an executive to obtain legal review is telling her something. The invention-assignment clause could transfer rights in an asset she has built for eight years; the cause definition makes much of the compensation contingent on one person’s satisfaction; and the CEO’s assurances are superseded by the entire-agreement clause. Spending $3,500 to understand a contract worth far more is cheap, and enforceability questions cannot be answered without a lawyer who knows the relevant states’ law.

perspectives.title: Stay, or walk away from this offer
perspectives.text: On a risk-adjusted basis the offer may be worth less than it looks. The discretionary bonus, repayable sign-on, illiquid equity and broad cause definition mean much of the headline value depends on Orrisbane’s goodwill, while the restrictions follow her for up to two years whatever happens. Pellucid’s counteroffer is smaller but more certain and far less restrictive. Declining is a legitimate outcome of good analysis, not a failure of nerve.

perspectives.title: The company’s view
perspectives.text: Orrisbane has legitimate interests: trade secrets, customer relationships, and the fact that Nadia’s library overlaps with its product roadmap. But terms this broad may be unenforceable in some states, may deter the strongest candidates and may sour the relationship before it begins. A well-advised company would protect the same interests with narrower tools — a clear license or contribution agreement for the library, a defined customer non-solicit, objective cause — and win the candidate.

case.application: In player development and baseball operations, the same pattern appears whenever a professional is offered an attractive role with loosely defined restrictions: a coach or analyst joining a new organization under confidentiality and ownership terms that cover methods, models and data; an outside specialist engaged by a club; or a staff member who builds tools or teaches outside work. The case’s lessons transfer directly. Separate the value of the offer from the cost of the restrictions; ask which interest each restriction protects; insist that oral assurances appear in the document; and obtain qualified advice in the governing jurisdiction before the deadline rather than after. From the organization’s side, clear and proportionate terms are part of recruiting, not only of risk control.

questions.prompt: A city health department is choosing between two ways to regulate food storage in restaurants. Option 1: “Refrigerated food must be held at or below a specified temperature.” Option 2: “Food must be stored at safe temperatures.” Thousands of near-identical inspections occur each year. Which statement best captures the trade-off in Kaplow’s analysis?

options.text: Option 1 is always better because precise laws are always better laws.
Option 1 costs more to set but is cheaper and more predictable to apply across thousands of similar inspections; Option 2 is cheaper to write but leaves its content to be worked out case by case.
Option 2 is better because inspectors are experts and rules prevent them from using their expertise.
There is no meaningful difference, because a court will interpret either one.

questions.explanation: Kaplow’s central point is about when the content of a law is supplied: before conduct (rules) or after it (standards). Rules carry higher up-front costs and lower application costs, so they tend to be efficient for frequent, homogeneous conduct such as routine inspections. Option 2 shifts the cost to every inspection and every dispute.

optionFeedback.a: Rules have real costs: they can be over- or under-inclusive, and they are not always worth their drafting cost when situations are rare and varied.
optionFeedback.c: Expertise can justify standards in rare, varied situations, but frequent, similar inspections are where rules pay off.
optionFeedback.d: Most rules are applied without any court involvement; the difference is in predictability and cost for everyone who must comply and enforce.

questions.prompt: Identify the most important flaw in this reasoning.

stimulus.text: A regional manager at a fictional beverage company writes: “We can terminate our distributor tomorrow without notice. Last year a court in another state held that a distributor could be terminated without notice. That decision settles the question for us. And since the distributor would have to prove we acted improperly, we have nothing to worry about.”

options.text: It treats an out-of-state decision as controlling, when it is at most persuasive and may be distinguishable on the contract terms or the governing law — and a favorable burden of proof does not eliminate risk.
It is flawed because courts never consider decisions from other states.
It is flawed because the company, not the distributor, always carries the burden of proof in contract disputes.
It is flawed because distributor relationships are governed only by federal law.

questions.explanation: Precedent binds only within its jurisdiction; an out-of-state case is persuasive at most, and it may involve a different contract and different governing law. The argument also misreads the burden of proof: it decides close cases, but the distributor may still be able to meet it, and litigation has costs regardless of who wins.

optionFeedback.b: Courts often consider other states’ decisions as persuasive authority; they are simply not bound by them.
optionFeedback.c: The party bringing a claim usually carries the burden; that part of the manager’s reasoning is not the main error.
optionFeedback.d: Distribution agreements are mainly governed by state contract law and, in some industries, by state statutes.

questions.prompt: Which analysis best reflects general U.S. contract principles?

stimulus.text: During a recruiting call, the chief executive of a fictional health-technology startup tells a senior engineer at a competitor: “If you join us, I’ll make sure you get a 2 percent equity grant.” The engineer resigns, turns down a counteroffer and joins. The written offer letter, signed after the call, says nothing about equity and states that it is the parties’ entire agreement. Six months later the board grants her 0.5 percent.

options.text: The chief executive’s statement is binding because it was made before the written letter.

The entire-agreement clause makes the signed letter the likely complete statement of terms, so the oral promise is hard to enforce as a contract term; reliance-based or misrepresentation arguments may exist but face real obstacles, and the outcome depends on the facts and state law.
Oral promises are never enforceable in employment.
She has a clear claim to 2 percent because she relied on the promise by resigning.

questions.explanation: An integration clause signals that the written document is the complete agreement, which makes earlier oral statements difficult to enforce as terms. Doctrines such as promissory estoppel or misrepresentation are not automatically excluded, but they face obstacles: a written integrated agreement, questions about how definite the promise was, and state-specific rules. The lesson for the reader is to put important promises in the document.

optionFeedback.a: Timing cuts the other way: an integration clause in a later signed writing generally supersedes earlier discussions.
optionFeedback.c: Oral agreements can be enforceable in some circumstances; the problem here is the integration clause and the later writing.
optionFeedback.d: Reliance strengthens a promissory-estoppel argument but does not make the claim clear, especially against an integrated written agreement.

questions.prompt: A hospital receives the clause below in a software vendor’s contract. Select every real issue it raises for the hospital.

stimulus.text: “Vendor warrants that the scheduling software will substantially conform to its documentation for 90 days after installation. Customer’s sole and exclusive remedy for any breach of this warranty is for Vendor to use commercially reasonable efforts to correct the nonconformity. Vendor’s total liability shall not exceed the fees paid in the three months before the claim.” (Fictional clause.)

options.text: The warranty period is short relative to the expected life of the software.
The exclusive remedy is an efforts obligation with no deadline and no refund or termination right if the fix fails.
The liability cap may be small relative to the harm a scheduling failure could cause.
The clause is unenforceable because all software warranties must last at least one year.
“Substantially conform to its documentation” depends on what the documentation says, so the documentation needs review.
Warranties in software contracts are prohibited by federal law.

questions.explanation: The clause gives a short, documentation-based warranty, a weak exclusive remedy and a low cap — each a real risk-allocation issue for a hospital that depends on scheduling. There is no general rule requiring one-year software warranties, and software warranties are not prohibited.

optionFeedback.a: Correct: 90 days may expire before many defects surface in a system used for years.
optionFeedback.b: Correct: an efforts-only exclusive remedy can leave the customer with a non-working system and no exit.
optionFeedback.c: Correct: three months of fees may be far below the operational cost of a failure.
optionFeedback.d: No general rule sets a minimum warranty period for software; this is invented.
optionFeedback.e: Correct: a warranty measured against documentation is only as good as the documentation.
optionFeedback.f: Software warranties are common and lawful; this statement is false.

questions.prompt: Rank these situations from the one that most urgently warrants involving counsel to the one that least warrants it.

options.text: A former employee’s lawyer sends a letter alleging discrimination and asking the company to preserve documents.
A vendor proposes a three-year, high-value exclusive agreement with an unusual indemnity clause.
A manager wants to update the internal form employees use to submit routine travel receipts.
A team wants to reuse a standard, previously approved non-disclosure agreement with a new prospective partner.

questions.explanation: A litigation threat with a preservation demand is urgent: deadlines, preservation duties and privileged communication all begin now. A high-value exclusive deal with unusual risk terms needs review before signature. Reusing an approved NDA is low risk but still a legal document; a routine internal form has the least legal content.

questions.prompt: Which interpretation of this fictional study is best supported?

stimulus.text: Fictional study. A state began enforcing non-competes for software workers in 2015; two neighboring states continued not to enforce them. Using payroll records, researchers compare the annual rate at which software workers changed employers before and after 2015. The authors conclude: “Enforcing non-competes reduced mobility by 3 percentage points, and therefore lowered wages and harmed innovation.”

stimulus.caption: Annual employer-change rate among software workers (fictional)
stimulus.note: Synthetic data for a fictional study.

options.text: The difference-in-differences comparison supports a reduction of about 3 percentage points in job-changing, if the groups would otherwise have followed parallel trends; the claims about wages and innovation go beyond what was measured.
The study proves non-competes lower wages, because lower mobility always means lower wages.
Because the study is not a randomized trial, it tells us nothing about non-competes.
A 3-point change is too small to matter, so non-competes have no effect.

questions.explanation: The design compares the change in the enforcing state with the change in comparison states, which supports a causal reading of the mobility estimate under the parallel-trends assumption. Wages and innovation were not measured, so those conclusions are speculation. This mirrors the strengths and limits of the Michigan study.

optionFeedback.b: Mobility and wages are related but distinct; the study measured only mobility.
optionFeedback.c: Natural experiments can support causal claims when their assumptions are plausible; dismissing all non-randomized evidence is too strong.
optionFeedback.d: A fall from 14 to 11 percent is a roughly one-fifth reduction in the rate; “small” requires an argument, and small effects can still matter.

questions.prompt: A software company wants to protect its source code and client relationships when engineers leave, without relying on a broad non-compete. Which of the following are narrower tools that can protect those interests? Select all that apply.

options.text: A confidentiality agreement with standard exclusions, backed by access controls and exit procedures.
A non-solicitation clause limited to clients the engineer actually worked with, for a defined period.
A clear invention-assignment clause covering work created within the scope of the job, with a schedule of excluded prior projects.
A clause forfeiting all salary already earned if the engineer joins any technology company.
A worldwide, five-year ban on working anywhere in software.
Garden leave for a small number of senior roles with access to strategic plans.

questions.explanation: Confidentiality with security, targeted client non-solicits, precise invention assignment and garden leave each address a specific interest — code, relationships, ownership, transition — with less restriction on the person’s ability to work. Forfeiting earned wages and five-year worldwide bans are neither narrow nor likely to be lawful or enforceable in many places.

optionFeedback.a: Correct: protects code and confidential information directly.
optionFeedback.b: Correct: protects the relationships at risk without barring all work.
optionFeedback.c: Correct: settles ownership of what the company paid for.
optionFeedback.d: Not narrow, and forfeiting wages already earned raises serious wage-law problems.
optionFeedback.e: The opposite of narrow; breadth like this invites unenforceability.
optionFeedback.f: Correct: a paid cooling-off period for the few roles that justify it.

questions.prompt: What is the best next move?

stimulus.text: You chair the selection committee at a fictional regional transit authority choosing a data-analytics vendor. The day before the vote, a committee member mentions that her brother is a senior executive at the lowest-priced bidder. She says she can be objective. The authority’s ethics policy requires disclosure of “any interest that could reasonably be seen to affect judgment” and names the general counsel as the decision-maker on conflicts. The board expects the contract approved this month.

options.text: Proceed with the vote; she has told you, and the lowest price is objectively best.

Ask her to put the disclosure in writing, refer it to the general counsel under the policy, have her step out of deliberations and the vote pending that decision, and document the process — delaying the vote briefly if necessary.
Disqualify the lowest-priced bidder to avoid any appearance of a conflict.
Keep the information confidential to spare her embarrassment, and vote against that bidder yourself to offset any bias.

questions.explanation: The policy assigns the conflict decision to the general counsel, not to the member or the chair. Written disclosure, recusal pending the decision and a documented process protect the integrity of the award and the bidder’s fair chance. A short delay costs little compared with a contested award.

optionFeedback.a: An oral mention to the chair does not satisfy a policy that names a different decision-maker, and price does not cure a process problem.
optionFeedback.c: Penalizing the bidder for a committee member’s relationship is unfair and may itself be challengeable; recusal addresses the conflict.
optionFeedback.d: Concealment converts a manageable conflict into an integrity problem, and voting to “offset” bias introduces your own.

questions.prompt: Which analysis best fits general agency principles?

stimulus.text: At a fictional media company, the Vice President of Partnerships has negotiated and signed several sponsorship agreements over two years, each honored by the company. A new internal policy requires the chief financial officer’s countersignature for deals above $250,000. The vice president signs a $400,000 sponsorship with a sports-streaming platform without the countersignature. The platform knew nothing of the policy. The company now wants out.

options.text: The company is not bound, because the vice president lacked actual authority.

The company may well be bound under apparent authority, because its own conduct — the title and the history of honored deals — reasonably led the platform to believe the vice president could sign; the internal policy mainly governs the company’s relationship with the vice president.
The contract is void because only a chief executive can sign contracts for a company.
Only the vice president is bound; organizations are never bound by contracts their agents sign.

questions.explanation: Apparent authority turns on what the principal’s conduct led a reasonable third party to believe. A title and a record of honored deals are classic sources of apparent authority, and an undisclosed internal limit does not usually defeat it. The company’s recourse is mainly internal.

optionFeedback.a: Lack of actual authority is not the end of the analysis; apparent authority can still bind the principal.
optionFeedback.c: Organizations routinely delegate signing authority; there is no general rule that only a CEO can sign.
optionFeedback.d: Agency law exists precisely because principals are bound by authorized — and apparently authorized — agents.

questions.prompt: A fictional marketing agency engages a consultant for 10 months at $12,000 per month, with no termination-for-convenience clause. After month 3 the agency ends the engagement without legal justification and stops paying. The consultant finds comparable replacement work starting in month 6, paying $9,000 per month through month 10. Using a simplified expectation measure that ignores costs saved, interest and legal fees, what are her damages for the remaining term, in dollars?
questions.working: Unpaid fees for months 4–10: 7 × $12,000 = $84,000. Mitigation earnings for months 6–10: 5 × $9,000 = $45,000. Simplified expectation damages: $84,000 − $45,000 = $39,000.
questions.explanation: Expectation damages aim to put her where full performance would have: the fees she would have earned for the remaining seven months, less what she earned (or reasonably could have earned) by mitigating. Ignoring costs saved, that is $84,000 minus $45,000, or $39,000. A termination-for-convenience clause would have cut this figure sharply.

questions.prompt: What is the best course of action?

stimulus.text: A product director at a fictional fintech company receives an email from in-house counsel analyzing whether a planned feature could violate consumer-protection rules. The director wants to share the analysis with (1) the three engineers building the feature, (2) an outside marketing agency preparing the launch campaign and (3) a reporter who has asked about the company’s approach to compliance.

options.text: Forward counsel’s email to all three groups so everyone has the same information.

Share the practical implications with the engineers who need them, ideally with counsel’s guidance; keep the email itself within the circle that needs the legal advice; ask counsel before sharing anything with the agency; and do not share the analysis with the reporter.
Mark the email “privileged” and forward it to all three groups; the label preserves the privilege.
Delete counsel’s email so that it cannot be requested later.

questions.explanation: Privilege depends on keeping legal-advice communications confidential among those who need them. Engineers implementing the advice can receive what they need; an outside agency is a third party, so counsel should decide what, if anything, it receives; a reporter is the clearest waiver. Labels do not create privilege, and deleting records can create far worse problems.

optionFeedback.a: Sending the advice to outsiders, especially a reporter, risks waiving privilege over the analysis.
optionFeedback.c: A label does not preserve confidentiality that the distribution itself destroys.
optionFeedback.d: Deleting relevant records can be treated as destruction of evidence if a dispute is anticipated, and it discards advice the company needs.

questions.prompt: A fictional consulting firm’s draft agreement with an independent consultant says: “All inventions, works and ideas that Consultant conceives during the Term, whether or not related to the Services, belong to the Firm.” The consultant maintains her own analytics toolkit, which she used before the engagement and will use during it. In 120–200 words: (1) explain the issue; (2) propose a plain-language redline; (3) write one specific question for counsel. (Self-assessed; educational exercise, not legal advice.)
questions.modelAnswer: The clause assigns everything the consultant conceives during the engagement, even work unrelated to the services, and it says nothing about her pre-existing toolkit. Because she will use the toolkit in the engagement and keep improving it, the clause invites a dispute over whether improvements made during the term — or the toolkit itself — now belong to the firm. It also reaches projects for other clients that the firm has not paid for. A plain-language redline: “The Firm owns the deliverables created specifically for it under this Agreement. Consultant keeps ownership of her pre-existing materials (listed in Schedule A), including improvements not made specifically for the Firm, and her general skills and know-how. To the extent pre-existing materials are built into a deliverable, Consultant grants the Firm a perpetual, non-exclusive license to use them as part of that deliverable.” Question for counsel: “Under the governing law, does a written license-back plus a schedule of pre-existing materials adequately protect the consultant’s ownership of the toolkit and its later improvements, and does any statute limit how far an assignment of a contractor’s unrelated work can reach?”

rubric.criterion: Identifies the issue: assignment of unrelated work and the unaddressed pre-existing toolkit
levels: 1 — Notes overbreadth or the toolkit, not both
2 — Explains both and why they create an ownership dispute

rubric.criterion: Proposes a plain-language redline that narrows ownership and preserves the firm’s legitimate interest
levels: 0 — No redline or simply deletes the clause
1 — Narrows ownership but ignores the firm’s need to use what it pays for
2 — Deliverables to the firm, pre-existing materials retained, license for embedded materials

rubric.criterion: Asks a specific question for counsel tied to governing law
levels: 1 — Specific question naming the law, the mechanism or the risk

reserve.prompt: In most U.S. civil lawsuits, what does the “preponderance of the evidence” standard require of the party with the burden of proof?

options.text: Proof beyond a reasonable doubt.
Proof that its version of the facts is more likely true than not.
Proof by at least two independent witnesses.
Clear and convincing evidence in every case.

reserve.explanation: Preponderance means more likely than not. Beyond a reasonable doubt is the criminal standard; clear and convincing evidence is an intermediate standard used for certain civil matters, such as fraud claims in many jurisdictions. No general two-witness rule applies.

optionFeedback.a: That is the criminal standard, far higher than the usual civil one.
optionFeedback.c: There is no general requirement of a particular number of witnesses.
optionFeedback.d: Clear and convincing evidence applies only to certain civil claims.

stimulus.text: In a fictional asset purchase, the seller’s agreement states that “all customer contracts are in full force and no customer has given notice of termination.” The statement is made as a representation and warranty, subject to a $500,000 indemnity cap and a 12-month survival period. Four months after closing, the buyer learns that a major customer had given notice of termination before closing.

options.text: The buyer has no remedy, because the deal has already closed.

The statement appears to have been untrue when made; the buyer’s recovery will depend largely on the indemnity terms — the cap, the survival period, any thresholds and qualifiers — and possibly on misrepresentation law.
The buyer can recover unlimited damages because the seller made a warranty.
The statement was a condition, so its failure simply excused the buyer from closing.

reserve.explanation: A representation and warranty that was false when made gives the buyer a claim, but the agreement’s own risk-allocation terms usually govern recovery: here a cap and a survival period that has not yet expired. Misrepresentation law may provide additional routes depending on the facts and jurisdiction.

optionFeedback.a: Survival periods exist precisely so that claims can be brought after closing.
optionFeedback.c: The contract caps recovery; warranty status does not override the cap.
optionFeedback.d: The accuracy of representations is often also a closing condition, but the deal closed; the remaining question is post-closing recovery.

reserve.prompt: As of November 2026, which statement best describes the FTC’s 2024 Non-Compete Clause Rule?

options.text: It is in force and makes most worker non-competes unenforceable nationwide.

It was set aside by a federal district court in August 2024; the FTC dismissed its appeals in September 2025 and the rule was removed from the Code of Federal Regulations in February 2026. Non-competes remain governed mainly by state law, and the FTC has said it may pursue individual cases.
The Supreme Court upheld it in 2025, so state non-compete laws no longer apply.
It was never finalized; the FTC only proposed it.

reserve.explanation: The final rule was published in May 2024 but set aside in Ryan LLC v. FTC on August 20, 2024, before its effective date. The Commission voted on September 5, 2025 to dismiss its appeals and accede to vacatur, and the rule’s text was later removed from the CFR. State law governs enforceability, and the FTC has said it will act case by case.

optionFeedback.a: The rule never took effect; it was set aside before its September 2024 effective date.
optionFeedback.c: No Supreme Court decision upheld the rule; the FTC abandoned its appeals.
optionFeedback.d: The rule was finalized and published in May 2024 before being set aside.

reserve.prompt: Which of the following are generally within a company’s attorney-client privilege? Select all that apply.

options.text: An employee’s confidential answers to a questionnaire sent by company counsel during an internal investigation, at management’s direction.
Counsel’s confidential legal advice to the executive team about a contract dispute.
The underlying facts of a workplace accident.
A business-strategy email on which counsel was merely copied.
Counsel’s advice after a manager forwarded it to an outside vendor not working with counsel.
A manager’s confidential email to counsel requesting legal advice about a termination.

reserve.explanation: Upjohn confirms that employees’ communications to counsel, made to secure legal advice for the company, can be privileged, as can counsel’s confidential advice and requests for it. Facts are never privileged, copying a lawyer does not convert business discussion into legal advice, and sharing with outsiders can waive protection.

optionFeedback.a: Correct: this is the situation Upjohn addressed.
optionFeedback.b: Correct: confidential legal advice to the client.
optionFeedback.c: Facts are not privileged, even if they were reported to counsel.
optionFeedback.d: Copying counsel does not make a business communication a request for legal advice.
optionFeedback.e: Disclosure to an outsider can waive the privilege.
optionFeedback.f: Correct: a confidential request for legal advice.

assignment.title: Issue-Spotting Memorandum: A Professional Services Agreement

brief.text: **Educational exercise on a fictional agreement — not legal advice.** Larkhaven, Quorvane and the agreement below are invented for teaching. Your memo practices how a business leader prepares a first-pass review for qualified counsel; it is not a legal opinion, it does not advise any real party, and it should not be used to review an actual agreement. Consult a qualified attorney about any specific agreement.

Larkhaven Regional Health (fictional), a nonprofit system of three hospitals, plans to hire Quorvane Insight Partners LLC (fictional) to build a patient-flow forecasting tool and train hospital staff to use it. Quorvane has sent its standard Professional Services Agreement, excerpted in Exhibit A. The chief operating officer has asked you, as the executive sponsoring the project, to prepare an issue-spotting memorandum for the general counsel before negotiations begin. The memo should identify legal and commercial issues from Larkhaven's perspective, rank them, explain why each matters, frame questions for counsel, propose plain-language redlines and set negotiation priorities.

brief.caption: Exhibit A — Excerpt from Quorvane’s Professional Services Agreement (fictional)
rows: Quorvane will perform the services described in the Proposal and such additional services as the parties may agree. Timelines in the Proposal are estimates only.
Fees are $42,000 per month, invoiced monthly in advance and payable within 15 days. Fees increase by 7% on each anniversary of the Effective Date.

The initial term is 24 months. The Agreement renews automatically for successive 12-month terms unless either party gives notice of non-renewal at least 120 days before the end of the then-current term.
Quorvane may terminate for convenience on 30 days' notice. Client may terminate only for Quorvane's material breach not cured within 60 days after written notice.
Deliverables are deemed accepted five business days after delivery unless Client provides a detailed written description of each nonconformity.

Quorvane retains all right, title and interest in the forecasting tool, models, code and documentation, including all modifications made for Client. Client receives a non-exclusive license to use the deliverables during the Term.
Client grants Quorvane a perpetual, irrevocable license to use Client Data, in de-identified or aggregated form, to improve Quorvane's products and services.

Quorvane may use subcontractors, including subcontractors located outside the United States, without Client's consent. Client will not hire any Quorvane personnel during the Term and for 24 months afterward; for any such hire, Client will pay Quorvane a fee equal to 100% of the individual's annual compensation.

Quorvane warrants that the Services will be performed in a professional manner. Except as stated in this Section, Quorvane disclaims all other warranties, including any warranty of the accuracy of forecasts.

Quorvane's total liability will not exceed the fees paid in the three months before the claim. Neither party is liable for indirect or consequential damages, including damages arising from any data breach.
Each party will protect the other's Confidential Information for two years after termination.
Disputes will be resolved by binding arbitration in Quorvane's home city under the law of Quorvane's home state.
brief.note: Fictional agreement written for this exercise. Not a model or recommended form.

brief.text: Assume Larkhaven's priorities are patient privacy, continuity of the tool after the contract ends, a predictable budget for three years and the ability to exit if the tool does not work. Larkhaven has two alternative vendors, both more expensive. The project is a board-level priority with a target start date four months away.

Your memo is a business document for counsel. Where an answer depends on law — for example, the privacy and security requirements that apply when a vendor handles patient information, or whether a no-hire fee is enforceable — say so and turn it into a question for counsel rather than guessing. Notice what the excerpt does not contain as well as what it does: obligations you would expect in a health-data engagement may be missing.

items: Rank issues by severity, using explicit criteria such as size of exposure, likelihood, and whether the exposure is bounded.
Distinguish legal questions (for counsel) from commercial ones (for you and the negotiating team).
Write redlines in plain language that a negotiator could put on the table, not formal drafting.
Separate must-haves, tradeables and acceptable terms, and say what you would offer in exchange.
Close with your assumptions and a one-line statement that the memo is not legal advice.

assignment.deliverable: A 900–1,300-word issue-spotting memorandum to the general counsel on the fictional Quorvane agreement, with ranked issues, reasons, questions for counsel, plain-language redlines and negotiation priorities.

template.heading: Bottom line
template.guidance: Two to four sentences: the agreement's overall risk posture for Larkhaven, the three issues that matter most, and what you need from counsel.

template.heading: Issues ranked by severity
template.guidance: A ranked list (high, medium, low) of 8–12 issues, each tied to a section of Exhibit A or to a missing term. State your ranking criteria.

template.heading: Why each matters
template.guidance: For each high and medium issue, the legal and commercial consequence for Larkhaven in plain language. Keep legal conclusions provisional.

template.heading: Questions for counsel
template.guidance: Five to eight specific questions only counsel can answer — governing law, enforceability, regulatory requirements — each with the facts counsel needs.

template.heading: Proposed redlines in plain language
template.guidance: For the top five issues, the change you would ask for, written as a short instruction or replacement sentence.

template.heading: Negotiation priorities
template.guidance: Must-haves, tradeables and acceptable terms; what you would offer in exchange; and your alternative if Quorvane refuses (Week 7).

template.heading: Assumptions and limits
template.guidance: What you assumed, what you did not know, and a one-line statement that this memo is not legal advice.

scenario.text: Larkhaven Regional Health (fictional), a nonprofit system of three hospitals, plans to hire Quorvane Insight Partners LLC (fictional) to build a patient-flow forecasting tool and train staff to use it. Quorvane has sent its standard Professional Services Agreement. As the executive sponsoring the project, you are preparing an issue-spotting memorandum for Larkhaven's general counsel before negotiations begin.

audience.cares: Precise issues tied to sections, the facts needed to answer legal questions, and a clear sense of business priorities so legal effort goes where it matters.
Whether the project can start on time, stay within budget and protect patients — and which few points could change the decision.

checklist: Bottom line in the first two sentences
Every issue tied to a section or to a named missing term
Legal questions separated from commercial ones
Redlines written in plain language a negotiator could use
States assumptions and that the memo is not legal advice

prompts: Recall an agreement you signed or approved in the past few years — an employment document, a vendor contract, a lease. Which clause do you now suspect you did not fully understand, and what question would you ask about it today?

Think of a policy in an organization you know that is written as a standard (“reasonable,” “appropriate”). Has it produced inconsistent decisions? Would a rule be better, and what would the rule cost?
When have you seen a lawyer brought in too late, or too early? What signal would have marked the right moment?
Where in your professional world do institutional constraints — regulation, collective agreements, league or association rules — quietly decide questions that look like individual choices?

review.front: When does Kaplow’s analysis favor a rule over a standard?
review.back: When the regulated conduct is frequent and similar, so the higher up-front cost of writing a rule is spread across many cases, and people can learn the rule before they act.

review.front: What are the steps of IRAC, and what does APERTURE add for executives?
review.back: Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion — plus consequence and confidence: the stakes, the probability and whether counsel is needed.

review.front: What is the usual standard of proof in a U.S. civil contract dispute, and who usually carries it?
review.back: Preponderance of the evidence (more likely than not), usually carried by the party bringing the claim.

review.front: Is a court bound by another state’s decision?
review.back: No. Precedent binds within a jurisdiction’s court hierarchy; out-of-state decisions are persuasive at most and can be distinguished on their facts.

review.front: What are the elements of contract formation, and what doctrine can substitute for consideration?
review.back: Offer, acceptance and bargained-for consideration (plus capacity and legality). Promissory estoppel can enforce some promises on the basis of reasonable reliance.

review.front: What happens when a condition fails, compared with when a promise is broken?
review.back: If a condition fails, the dependent duty never arises — there is no breach. A broken promise is a breach that can support damages.

review.front: Why might a buyer prefer a warranty to a representation of the same fact?
review.back: A warranty is a promise backed by a remedy and generally does not require proof that the seller was at fault; a misrepresentation claim can require more.
Foreseeability when the contract was made, reasonable certainty and the duty to mitigate — and, in practice, the contract’s own caps, exclusive remedies and termination rights.

review.front: What does at-will employment mean, and what limits it?
review.back: Either party may end employment at any time for any lawful reason; limited by anti-discrimination and retaliation statutes, public-policy exceptions, individual contracts and collective agreements.

review.front: What happened to the FTC’s 2024 non-compete rule?
review.back: Published May 7, 2024; set aside by a Texas federal court on August 20, 2024, before taking effect; the FTC voted on September 5, 2025 to drop its appeals; the rule was removed from the CFR in February 2026. State law still governs.

review.front: What did the Michigan non-compete natural experiment find?
review.back: After Michigan began enforcing non-competes in 1985, inventor mobility fell about 8 percent relative to comparison states, more for specialists and for inventors with firm-specific skills (Marx, Strumsky and Fleming, 2009).

review.front: Who owns copyright in an independent contractor’s work if the contract says nothing?
review.back: Generally the contractor, absent a signed assignment or a qualifying work-made-for-hire agreement; the client may have an implied right to use what it paid for.
Authority a third party reasonably infers from the principal’s own conduct — a title, past dealings — which can bind the principal even when the agent exceeded internal limits.

review.front: Why did the directors in Smith v. Van Gorkom lose the protection of the business judgment rule?
review.back: They approved a merger without informing themselves of reasonably available information; the court found gross negligence in the process — a breach of the duty of care — even though the price was a premium.

review.front: What did Upjohn Co. v. United States (1981) decide about corporate privilege?
review.back: Privilege can cover communications between corporate counsel and employees below senior management, made to secure legal advice for the company; the Court rejected the narrow “control group” test.

review.front: Name three habits that protect privilege.
review.back: Keep legal-advice communications to those who need them; keep legal and business discussion in separate threads; never forward or summarize counsel’s advice outside that circle without asking.

preview.text: Week 12 turns strategy into execution. Implementation plans depend on vendor contracts, data agreements and clear decision rights, so this week’s issue-spotting habits carry directly into project governance. Week 13 returns to governance from the ethical side — conflicts of interest, accountability and the responsible use of data — and asks what to do when an action is lawful but questionable. The capstone in Week 14 integrates behavior, strategy, law and leadership, and expects you to name the legal and institutional constraints on any recommendation and the questions that belong to counsel.

links.why: Negotiation priorities, alternatives and concessions decide which contract terms are worth fighting for.
Vendor agreements, decision rights and implementation governance.
Conflicts of interest, accountability and the gap between lawful and right.
The capstone asks you to surface legal and institutional constraints on a strategic proposal.
